translationNote: All 374 questions have English draft translations. Questions 1–4 were checked with Google Translate; the remaining translations are AI-assisted drafts and require human review before release.

questions.prompt: "The system MUST use OAuth 2.0 for authentication." A requirements engineer classifies this as a constraint. Which statement is correct?
options: The classification is incorrect, as any specification formulated with ‘must’ is, by definition, a functional requirement.
The classification is correct: OAuth 2.0 limits the solution space (only this protocol is permitted) and is therefore a constraint, regardless of who formulated it.
The classification depends on whether OAuth 2.0 was proposed by the client or by the development team.
OAuth 2.0 is always a security-related quality requirement, since authentication concerns the quality attribute ‘security’.
questions.explanation: A constraint limits the solution space—specifying a particular protocol rules out all alternatives. If the requirement had simply stated ‘authentication is required,’ it would be a functional requirement. The source of the specification (client vs. team) is irrelevant to its classification. Security, as a quality attribute, describes the quality of a function, not a restriction on the choice of implementation.

questions.prompt: Which of the following requirements is most clearly classified as a QUALITY REQUIREMENT rather than a constraint?
options: The system must be operated using PostgreSQL 15 as its database.
The system must ensure that 99.5% of all booking requests are answered within 1 second.
The system must operate in a certified ISO 27001 environment.
The system may only use open-source libraries with an MIT license.
questions.explanation: The 99.5% response time describes a measurable quality attribute of the system (performance/reliability)—a quality requirement. PostgreSQL, the ISO 27001 environment, and the license requirement all limit the solution space; they are constraints. A quality requirement describes HOW WELL the system does something, while a constraint dictates an implementation decision.

questions.prompt: An authority stipulates: ‘The system may only be operated on servers physically located within the EU.’ What is the PRIMARY requirement type?
options: Quality requirement (data protection compliance), because it concerns the system’s security and GDPR compliance.
Functional requirement, because it describes what the system must achieve.
Constraint, because a technical and legal requirement restricts the solution space.
Need-level stakeholder requirement, because it was formulated by an external party.
questions.explanation: The server-location rule limits the solution space—hosting options outside the EU are excluded. This is a constraint. Although GDPR compliance is a quality attribute, this specific requirement describes an implementation restriction, not a measurable quality of the system. The type of issuing party (authority) does not determine the requirement category.

questions.prompt: Which statement most precisely describes the term SYSTEM CONTEXT in the IREB sense?
options: The system context is the part of the system environment relevant to the system being developed—factors outside the system boundary that influence or are influenced by the system.
The system context includes all technical components that the system requires during execution.
The system context is identical to the system architecture and defines which modules the system contains.
The system context describes only the human users and their interactions with the system.
questions.explanation: The system context is explicitly the relevant part of the environment OUTSIDE the system boundary. It includes external systems, stakeholders, regulations, and processes that influence or are influenced by the system. Technical components, architecture, and modules belong to the system itself, not its context.

questions.prompt: A project manager claims: ‘The four core IREB activities of the RE process are elicitation, documentation, design, and management.’ What is wrong with this statement?
options: Nothing—according to IREB Syllabus v3, design is a full core RE activity.
Design is not a core RE activity; the fourth activity is verification/validation. Design belongs to systems engineering.
According to IREB, there is no fixed number of core activities; the list is arbitrary.
Management is not a core activity; the correct fourth activity is modeling.
questions.explanation: The four IREB core activities are elicitation, documentation, verification/validation, and management. Design is an activity of systems engineering or software architecture—it is outside RE. Modeling is part of documentation, not a separate core activity.

questions.prompt: Which RE activity checks whether the specification corresponds to stakeholders’ actual needs?
options: Verification—checks whether the code compiles without errors.
Validation—checks whether the specification matches stakeholder needs (‘Are we building the RIGHT system?’).
Documentation—creates the specification.
Prioritization—ranks requirements by importance.
questions.explanation: Validation answers ‘Are we building the RIGHT system?’—it checks whether the specification covers stakeholders’ real needs. Verification answers ‘Are we building the system RIGHT?’—it checks whether the implementation conforms to the specification.

questions.prompt: A requirements engineering team is gathering requirements for a tax return system. Tax advisors ‘can hardly put their work steps into words.’ The budget is tight, and stakeholders are short on time. Which elicitation strategy offers the best compromise?
options: A structured interview with a prepared questionnaire—cost-effective and quick, even though tacit knowledge may remain hidden.
A simple paper prototype of the core workflows, accompanied by short feedback sessions—externalizes tacit knowledge at a manageable cost.
Several weeks of ethnographic field observation of all tax advisors—maximum insight, although the effort is high.
Analysis only of existing tax forms—uses available sources without burdening stakeholders.
questions.explanation: Low-fidelity prototyping combines the most important strengths: it externalizes tacit knowledge that interviews cannot uncover, at considerably lower effort than ethnography. A questionnaire fails because of the nature of the problem (tacit knowledge). Document analysis alone misses process details. Ethnography would be ideal, but is not feasible with a tight budget—the trade-off clearly favors prototyping.

questions.prompt: A reviewer objects: ‘The external payroll system is listed as an actor—that is wrong, because actors can only be people.’ Which statement is correct?
options: The reviewer is right: in UML, actors are always human user roles.
The reviewer is mistaken: external systems can also be actors if they operate outside the system boundary and interact with the system.
The reviewer is right, but only when the external system operates fully automatically without human involvement.
The reviewer is partly mistaken: external systems may be actors, but they must be labeled ‘secondary actors’.
questions.explanation: According to UML and IREB, actors are roles outside the system boundary that interact with the system—people, organizations, or external systems. Restricting actors to people is a common misconception. Options C and D contain plausible-sounding details that are not prescribed by the IREB standard.

questions.prompt: A requirement states: ‘The system must correctly process 99.9% of all requests.’ A requirements engineer considers it testable because it contains a percentage. What quality problem still remains?
options: The requirement is too short and needs to be written in greater detail.
99.9% sounds precise, but without a defined measurement period it is not testable: does this apply daily, monthly, or yearly? The resulting values differ greatly.
The requirement violates atomicity because it combines two aspects (correctness and availability).
The requirement is inconsistent with typical SLAs and must be adjusted to industry standards.
questions.explanation: A number alone does not make a requirement testable. Without a measurement period, 99.9% could mean about 86 incorrectly processed requests per day or about 720 per month. The test context is missing. Options A and D address real but secondary issues. Option C is factually incorrect: correctness and processing rate are not separate requirement aspects here.

questions.prompt: A team must change REQ-047. Traceability links connect REQ-047 to test cases TC-012 and TC-031, and to design element DE-07. What is the PRIMARY benefit of these links for the change?
options: The links automatically update TC-012, TC-031, and DE-07 as soon as REQ-047 is changed.
The links identify all artifacts that may be affected by changing REQ-047, providing a basis for impact analysis.
The links prevent REQ-047 from being changed until the Change Control Board has approved it.
The links ensure that REQ-047 still reflects the original stakeholder needs.
questions.explanation: Traceability links support impact analysis: which test cases, design elements, and other requirements are affected by a change? This is their primary benefit when managing changes. Automatic updates (A) and approval gates (C) are separate processes; stakeholder validation (D) is a different RE activity.

questions.prompt: Which elicitation technique is best suited to externalizing TACIT KNOWLEDGE that stakeholders cannot directly put into words?
options: A structured interview with a questionnaire.
Analysis of existing process manuals.
Field observation or prototyping.
A questionnaire distributed by email.
questions.explanation: Field observation and prototyping externalize tacit knowledge. During observation, stakeholders reveal workflows they may not be able to articulate. With a prototype, they respond to a model and identify what is missing or incorrect. Interviews and questionnaires are limited by the difficulty of verbalizing this knowledge.

questions.prompt: Which notation is suitable for modeling an object’s STATES and the events that trigger transitions between those states?
options: Use-case diagram.
Activity diagram.
State machine diagram.
Sequence diagram.
questions.explanation: A state machine models an object’s states and the events that trigger transitions. Use-case diagrams provide an overview of functionality; activity diagrams model process flows; sequence diagrams show interaction sequences between components.

questions.prompt: A requirement says: ‘The system should be fast, secure, and user-friendly.’ Which quality criterion is violated MOST SEVERELY?
options: Consistency—‘fast’ and ‘secure’ often conflict with one another.
Testability—none of the three adjectives includes a measurable threshold.
Atomicity—three different quality attributes are bundled into a single requirement.
Completeness—the requirement contains no technical implementation details.
questions.explanation: Although testability is also violated (there are no measurable values), the most serious issue is the violation of atomicity: performance, security, and usability are three distinct quality attributes that should be prioritized, tested, and managed separately. Atomicity is a structural prerequisite for the other quality criteria.

questions.prompt: Which review technique is characterized by an AUTHOR PRESENTATION and spontaneous reviewer feedback without structured preparation?
options: Formal inspection (Fagan inspection).
Walkthrough.
Technical review.
Informal peer review by email.
questions.explanation: In a walkthrough, the author presents the document and reviewers give spontaneous feedback—there are no prepared checklists or defect metrics. A formal inspection requires individual preparation. A technical review lies between the two in formality.

questions.prompt: A reviewer objects: ‘The internal accountant cannot be shown as an actor because they are an employee of the company—actors must be external.’ Which statement is correct?
options: The reviewer is right—only people outside the company can be actors.
The reviewer is mistaken: the SYSTEM BOUNDARY matters, not the company boundary. An employee who uses the system from outside it is a valid actor.
The reviewer is right, but only if the accountant does not have administrator access.
The reviewer is partly mistaken: employees may be actors, but must be labeled ‘internal actors’ to distinguish them from external actors.
questions.explanation: The definition of an actor is based on the system boundary, not the company boundary. An employee using the system acts from outside the system and is therefore a valid actor. Options C and D contain plausible-sounding distinctions that are not part of the IREB standard.

questions.prompt: A specification contains 200 numbered requirements, but REQ-015 is missing without explanation. Which quality criterion of the SPECIFICATION (not of an individual requirement) is violated?
options: Specification consistency—the gap may imply hidden contradictions.
Specification completeness—all necessary requirements must be documented.
Unambiguity—REQ-015 could be interpreted in different ways.
Testability—certain test cases cannot be created without REQ-015.
questions.explanation: A missing requirement violates the completeness of the specification (document level). Completeness means that all necessary requirements are included. Consistency and unambiguity concern the content of existing requirements, not gaps. Testability is a characteristic of individual requirements.

questions.prompt: A requirements engineer notices that stakeholder answers depend strongly on how questions are worded. In which interview format can this bias occur most systematically?
options: Unstructured interview—open questions encourage free-form accounts.
Structured interview with fixed leading questions—a flawed questionnaire creates the same bias for every respondent.
Semi-structured interview—a flexible guide allows follow-up questions.
The bias is independent of the format and is caused solely by the interviewer.
questions.explanation: A structured interview uses the same questionnaire with every stakeholder. If it contains leading questions, it introduces the same distortion for each respondent—systematic bias at scale. Questions vary in an unstructured interview, while a semi-structured interview allows room for adjustment.

questions.prompt: A project manager adds a feature enhancement directly to the specification without an approval process. What is the most serious change-management violation?
options: The stakeholder should have submitted the request in writing before communicating it verbally.
The change was added to the baseline without an impact analysis and formal approval by an authorized body.
The development team should first have checked technical feasibility.
The enhancement should first have been agreed with all stakeholders.
questions.explanation: Change management requires: (1) a documented request, (2) an impact analysis covering scope, cost, quality, and schedule, (3) a decision by an authorized body such as a Change Control Board, and (4) implementation with updates to affected artifacts. Adding the change directly skips the first three steps and destabilizes the agreed baseline.

questions.prompt: An English-language requirement says: ‘The system should encrypt all passwords at rest.’ What is the correct interpretation of this modal verb?
options: ‘Should’ indicates a binding obligation—it must be implemented.
‘Should’ means recommended but not mandatory; ‘shall’ should be used for a mandatory requirement.
‘Should’ and ‘shall’ are interchangeable in modern specifications because both express urgency.
‘Should’ is stronger than ‘shall’ because it expresses an ethical obligation.
questions.explanation: According to ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148 and RFC 2119, ‘shall’ means mandatory, ‘should’ means recommended but not required, and ‘may’ means optional. Encrypting passwords at rest is a critical security requirement; using ‘should’ leaves legal and technical discretion that may be problematic in practice.

questions.prompt: A Scrum team claims: ‘In our agile project, structured requirements engineering is unnecessary—we clarify everything directly in sprint planning with the Product Owner.’ Which assessment is most accurate?
options: The claim is correct—Scrum ceremonies completely replace all IREB RE activities.
The claim is true for small teams, but does not scale beyond 10 people.
The claim is incomplete—RE activities take place in Scrum but are distributed: elicitation in refinement, validation in the sprint review, and management in the backlog.
The claim is false: Scrum projects must create a complete requirements specification before the first sprint.
questions.explanation: Requirements engineering is not absent from agile projects; it is adapted. Elicitation occurs during backlog refinement, documentation uses user stories and acceptance criteria, validation takes place in sprint reviews and retrospectives, and management is handled through the prioritized Product Backlog. IREB emphasizes that RE activities exist independently of the development approach.

questions.prompt: Which elements belong to the SYSTEM CONTEXT according to IREB?
options: Only people who use the system directly (direct end users).
All elements outside the system boundary that influence or are influenced by the system.
All internal subsystems and database components of the system.
Only external stakeholders who participate in RE workshops.
questions.explanation: The system context consists of all relevant elements OUTSIDE the system boundary: external systems, stakeholders, regulations, and the physical environment. Whether they participate in the project is irrelevant; what matters is their mutual influence with the system.

questions.prompt: A specification contains REQ-12, ‘All customer data must be archived for 10 years’ (a compliance requirement), and REQ-47, ‘All customer data must be deleted after 2 years under the GDPR.’ How should a requirements engineer proceed?
options: Automatically prefer REQ-47 because it is newer and remove REQ-12 from the specification.
Document the contradiction, mark it as an open conflict, and escalate it to the relevant stakeholders for resolution.
Keep both requirements in the specification and let the development team find a technical solution.
Automatically prefer the requirement with the higher priority.
questions.explanation: A requirements engineer should not resolve conflicts unilaterally because the decision requires domain knowledge and authority (here, compliance and data-protection expertise). Contradictions must be documented and escalated. Option C is a common but dangerous workaround that wrongly transfers decision responsibility to the development team.

questions.prompt: A requirements team wants to visualize the system boundary and external data-exchange partners for a sales system. What does a CONTEXT DIAGRAM (DFD Level 0) show?
options: The internal database structure, including all entities and foreign-key relationships.
The system as a single process, all external entities, and the data flows crossing the system boundary.
All internal subprocesses and data stores within the system.
The chronological sequence of transactions between two systems over a communication channel.
questions.explanation: A Level-0 DFD (context diagram) shows the system as a black-box process, all external entities, and all data flows across the system boundary. Internal details, database structures, and process sequences appear only in more detailed DFD levels.

questions.prompt: A use case ‘Create invoice’ has an <<include>> relationship to ‘Verify customer data’. What does this mean for execution?
options: ‘Verify customer data’ runs only if an error occurs while ‘Create invoice’ is executing.
‘Verify customer data’ is executed completely and obligatorily every time ‘Create invoice’ is invoked.
‘Verify customer data’ is optional and is included only at the user’s explicit request.
Both use cases share an actor and can be triggered independently depending on the user’s role.
questions.explanation: <<include>> models a mandatory dependency: the base use case always includes the referenced use case. Conditional execution would be modeled with <<extend>>. Option A describes an error-triggered extension, not an include relationship.

questions.prompt: When is an <<extend>> relationship the CORRECT choice in a use-case diagram?
options: When use case A must always be fully embedded in use case B for B to achieve its goal.
When use case A optionally adds steps to base use case B under specified conditions.
When use cases A and B share the same primary actor.
When use case A replaces use case B in a newer system version.
questions.explanation: <<extend>> models optional additions under defined conditions (extension points), for example offering installment payments only when an amount exceeds a threshold. <<include>> is mandatory. Shared actors and replacement are not criteria for <<extend>>.

questions.prompt: A requirements engineer creates a stakeholder map for a logistics system and identifies end users and the client. Which important stakeholder groups are commonly overlooked?
options: External consultants supporting the project, who directly influence requirements engineering.
Regulators, IT operations, data-protection officers, and supplier systems—indirect stakeholders with legitimate requirements.
The development team, which must implement the requirements.
The test team, which validates the implementation and has specific requirements.
questions.explanation: Indirect stakeholders are often overlooked: customs authorities have compliance requirements; IT operations has maintainability and operational needs; data-protection officers address GDPR; and interface partners have technical requirements. A stakeholder map must go beyond direct users. Consultants, developers, and testers are generally identified more readily.

questions.prompt: A requirements management tool offers versioning, traceability links, automatic code generation, and status tracking. Which feature is ATYPICAL of an RM tool?
options: Versioning requirements.
Traceability links to test cases.
Automatically generating code from requirement text.
Tracking requirement status.
questions.explanation: RM tools specialize in management, versioning, traceability, and status tracking. Automatic code generation belongs to model-driven engineering tools. Expecting that feature in an RM tool confuses two different tool categories.

questions.prompt: ‘The system must be intuitive to use.’ Why is this NOT yet a finished system requirement?
options: ‘Intuitive’ is a complete and testable system property.
‘Intuitive’ is a stakeholder-level need that must be translated into measurable system requirements (for example, ‘80% of first-time users complete task X on their first attempt’).
Stakeholder and system requirements describe the same level.
‘Intuitive’ is already as precise as possible because usability cannot be quantified.
questions.explanation: ‘Intuitive’ is not testable because it has no measurable threshold. System requirements must be concrete and verifiable, such as measurable usability metrics. Stakeholder requirements express goals; requirements engineering translates them into testable system requirements.

questions.prompt: Which statement most precisely describes CONSISTENCY in a requirements specification?
options: All requirements use uniform wording templates and the same document style.
No requirement in the specification contradicts another requirement in that specification.
All requirements have the same level of detail and abstraction.
All requirements were reviewed and approved by the same stakeholders.
questions.explanation: Consistency is a content criterion: requirements must not contradict one another. Uniform templates concern readability and format; equal detail is a structural characteristic; and common approval is a process characteristic.

questions.prompt: In a Fagan inspection, which phase takes place immediately BEFORE the inspection meeting?
options: Rework—fixing defects from the previous cycle.
Follow-up—checking whether corrections are correct.
Individual preparation—each reviewer examines the document independently beforehand.
Planning—setting inspection objectives and selecting reviewers.
questions.explanation: Fagan inspection phases are planning, overview, individual preparation, inspection meeting, rework, and follow-up. Individual preparation immediately precedes the meeting and is a defining feature of a formal inspection.

questions.prompt: What is a typical LIMITATION of field observation as an elicitation technique?
options: It cannot capture explicitly documented requirements.
It provides only quantitative data about system usage.
It requires physical presence on site and can be difficult with globally distributed stakeholders when there is no travel budget.
It is suitable only for agile projects.
questions.explanation: Field observation requires physical presence. For globally distributed teams without a travel budget, this can be logistically impractical. Remote interviews, video shadowing, or questionnaires may be more feasible, although they may not capture tacit knowledge as effectively.

questions.prompt: What is the ESSENTIAL outcome of successful requirements negotiation?
options: All requirements from the most influential stakeholder are accepted.
The development team persuades the business to remove all optional requirements.
A compromise or prioritized consensus acceptable to all parties and feasible within the given constraints.
A complete, signed requirements specification containing everything discussed.
questions.explanation: Requirements negotiation aims for an accepted consensus; no single party should simply prevail. The requirements engineer facilitates priority discussions and compromises. A complete specification may result from later documentation, but is not itself the negotiation outcome.

questions.prompt: Which UML diagram shows ONLY a system’s static structure—classes, attributes, and relationships—with no temporal or behavioral dimension?
options: State machine diagram.
Sequence diagram.
Class diagram.
Activity diagram.
questions.explanation: A class diagram models static structure: classes or entities, their attributes, and relationships such as association, aggregation, composition, and generalization. It has no temporal dimension. State machines, sequence diagrams, and activity diagrams are dynamic notations.

questions.prompt: An agile team asks: ‘Do we need a formal requirements specification, or are user stories enough?’ Which answer is most appropriate?
options: User stories completely replace formal specifications; agile teams need no RE documentation.
Formal specifications are always necessary; even agile projects must create a complete requirements document.
It depends on the context: regulated domains or fixed-price contracts may legally require formal documentation; agile stories are sufficient in many other contexts.
User stories are only for development, while formal specifications are only for analysis.
questions.explanation: There is no universal answer. Formal documentation may be legally required in regulated domains such as medical technology or aviation. In agile startups without regulatory requirements, user stories may be sufficient. IREB competence includes making this judgment according to context.

questions.prompt: What best describes PERSPECTIVE-BASED READING as a review technique?
options: Each reviewer reads the same document three times from their own subjective perspective.
Reviewers read a document from a defined role (such as tester, designer, or operator) to find role-specific defects and gaps.
Only stakeholders from one particular department may participate in a review.
The same document is checked for consistency across several languages.
questions.explanation: Perspective-based reading assigns each reviewer a clearly defined role. A tester looks for untestable requirements, a designer for architectural conflicts, and an operator for missing maintenance requirements. These focused perspectives find role-specific defects more efficiently than general, unstructured reading.

questions.prompt: What most clearly distinguishes a formal INSPECTION from a TECHNICAL REVIEW?
options: Inspections always have more participants than technical reviews.
A formal inspection has strict phases, defined roles (moderator ≠ author), structured preparation, and defect metrics; a technical review is less formal.
Technical reviews examine only source code, while inspections examine only requirements documents.
Formal inspections require external reviewers; technical reviews use only internal experts.
questions.explanation: The main distinction is the degree of formality. Fagan inspections have mandatory phases, separated roles, checklists, and metrics. Technical reviews are more flexible and focus on technical correctness without the full formal process. Participant count and artifact type are not defining differences.

questions.prompt: A team is discussing numeric IDs (REQ-001) versus descriptive IDs (REQ-LOGIN-001). What is the primary trade-off?
options: Numeric IDs are more stable during restructuring; descriptive IDs improve orientation without lookup. Either approach can be appropriate depending on context.
Descriptive IDs are always better because they are understandable without a glossary.
Numeric IDs are required by ISO standards; descriptive IDs are prohibited in regulated projects.
Descriptive IDs make traceability links unnecessary because the context is already in the name.
questions.explanation: Numeric IDs are stable: REQ-001 remains REQ-001 even if the requirement moves. Descriptive IDs can lose meaning when a requirement changes category, but they make navigation in large specifications easier. Neither approach is mandated by ISO, and names do not replace traceability links.

questions.prompt: A stakeholder asks whether requirements in the ‘Won’t have’ category are permanently removed from the project. What is the correct answer?
options: ‘Won’t have’ means permanent exclusion; these requirements will not appear in any future release.
‘Won’t have (this time)’ means intentionally excluded from this release; they may be reconsidered in future releases.
‘Won’t have’ is the same as low priority and means the requirements will be implemented last in the project.
The development team always decides ‘Won’t have’ unilaterally without informing stakeholders.
questions.explanation: The full MoSCoW term is ‘Won’t have THIS TIME’—the qualifier matters. It is a scope-management tool for deferring, not discarding, requirements. This supports transparent expectations and focuses resources without implying permanent rejection.

questions.prompt: A Scrum team completes every story in a sprint, but the Product Owner is dissatisfied because the features do not meet expectations. Which RE activity was insufficient?
options: Backlog prioritization—the wrong stories were implemented first.
Estimation—the story points were too optimistic.
Validation—acceptance criteria were not adequately defined or checked during the sprint review.
Documentation—the stories were worded too briefly.
questions.explanation: Dissatisfaction despite completing all stories is a classic sign of insufficient validation. Inadequate acceptance criteria leave room for differing interpretations. The sprint review is the validation point for checking whether the result meets expectations. The other options are distractors in this scenario.

questions.prompt: What is the main difference between EXPLICIT and TACIT KNOWLEDGE in requirements engineering?
options: Explicit knowledge is always more important than tacit knowledge during elicitation.
Explicit knowledge is documented and directly accessible; tacit knowledge is embedded in experience and habits and often cannot be consciously articulated by stakeholders.
Tacit knowledge is found only among technical experts, while explicit knowledge is found only among managers.
Explicit knowledge exists only in written sources, while tacit knowledge exists only in oral accounts.
questions.explanation: Explicit knowledge is codified in manuals, contracts, or regulations and can be accessed through document analysis or direct questions. Tacit knowledge is embedded in practice, experience, and intuition: stakeholders may know it but be unable to articulate it. Field observation and prototyping help uncover it.

questions.prompt: ‘As a registered user, I want to reset my password so that I can regain access.’ A colleague says, ‘That is not a real user story—it contains technical details.’ Is the colleague correct?
options: Yes—user stories must not contain any system-specific terms.
No: the story follows the standard role/goal/benefit format, contains no implementation details, and is a valid user story.
Yes, because user stories apply only to new features, not security mechanisms.
Partly: the story is valid, but the benefit clause (‘so that’) is unnecessary and should be removed.
questions.explanation: ‘Reset my password’ describes functionality from the user’s perspective, not implementation details such as a transport protocol or encryption algorithm. The story follows the standard format. The colleague confuses a functional description with a technical specification. The benefit clause is an important part of the user-story concept.

questions.prompt: What is the PRIMARY purpose of a requirement ID (for example, REQ-042)?
options: To signal a requirement’s importance—lower IDs have higher priority.
To make each requirement uniquely referenceable so traceability links, change requests, and test cases can refer to it precisely.
To ensure requirements are implemented in ID order.
To automatically encode MoSCoW priority.
questions.explanation: Requirement IDs provide unique references—for example, linking REQ-042 to a test case or change request. IDs do not imply priority or implementation order; those are separate attributes. IDs underpin traceability.

questions.prompt: What is the ESSENTIAL difference between the KANO MODEL and the MOSCOW METHOD for requirements prioritization?
options: Kano is suitable only for agile projects; MoSCoW only for traditional projects.
MoSCoW prioritizes release necessity; Kano classifies requirements by their effect on customer satisfaction (basic, performance, and excitement attributes).
MoSCoW is used only for functional requirements; Kano only for quality requirements.
Kano is quantitative, whereas MoSCoW is qualitative and therefore less precise.
questions.explanation: MoSCoW classifies release urgency as Must, Should, Could, or Won’t. Kano classifies the psychological effect on customer satisfaction: basic attributes, performance attributes, and excitement attributes. The methods are complementary.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is a REQUIREMENTS ARTIFACT (RE artifact)?
options: A development team’s sprint burndown chart.
A JUnit test result after the latest sprint.
A System Requirements Specification (SRS) containing the documented requirements.
A CI/CD deployment-pipeline script.
questions.explanation: An RE artifact is a work product created during requirements engineering, such as a requirements specification, use-case description, glossary, traceability matrix, context diagram, or stakeholder map. The other options belong to project management, testing, or development/DevOps.

questions.prompt: An audit finds that 12 of 47 requirements cannot be traced to a stakeholder source, regulation, or business requirement. What traceability problem is present?
options: Missing forward traceability—requirements cannot be traced to test cases.
Missing backward traceability—requirements cannot be traced to their sources.
Inconsistent traceability—requirements contradict their sources.
Missing horizontal traceability—requirements are not linked to other requirements.
questions.explanation: Backward traceability connects each requirement to its source, such as a stakeholder need, regulation, or business goal. Requirements without sources are orphaned: they are difficult to justify or prioritize and may cause audit problems. Forward traceability links requirements to implementation and tests.

questions.prompt: What is the FIRST step in formal change management after a change request is received?
options: Implement it immediately if the change appears technically trivial.
Document the change request and perform an impact analysis.
Reject it because requirements cannot be changed after a baseline is agreed.
Directly inform stakeholders about the planned change.
questions.explanation: A formal change process begins by documenting the request and analyzing impacts on artifacts, cost, and schedule. An authorized body then evaluates and decides on the request, followed by implementation and updates to affected artifacts. Immediate implementation or rejection without analysis violates the process.

questions.prompt: The project manager declares the current requirements status to be the BASELINE. What applies to later changes?
options: No further changes are allowed after the baseline; the specification is frozen.
All subsequent changes must go through the formal change process and be documented against the baseline.
The baseline is informal and does not prevent the team from changing requirements directly.
A baseline means requirements must now be divided into sprints and implemented.
questions.explanation: A baseline is an agreed and approved state, not a freeze. Changes remain possible but must follow a controlled process of submission, analysis, approval, and documentation. The goal is traceability and stability, not immutability.

questions.prompt: In a SAFe project, requirements are documented as epics, features, and user stories. How does this relate to IREB core RE activities?
options: SAFe replaces the IREB RE process with an unrelated methodology.
IREB RE activities still occur in SAFe but are distributed: elicitation in PI Planning, validation in iteration reviews, and management through the backlog.
IREB RE applies only to waterfall projects; structured RE is absent in SAFe.
SAFe uses only informal techniques, without structured elicitation or documentation.
questions.explanation: IREB RE is methodology-agnostic: its four core activities occur in all development approaches, though artifacts, roles, and timing differ. In SAFe, elicitation occurs in PI Planning and refinement, documentation uses the epic-feature-story hierarchy, validation occurs in iteration reviews and system demos, and management uses prioritized backlogs.

questions.prompt: What is the primary goal of stakeholder analysis in requirements engineering?
options: To agree on the system’s technical architecture with all stakeholders.
To identify all people, groups, and organizations that provide requirements or are affected by the outcome.
To reconcile the project budget with stakeholder interests.
To define communication channels between the development team and the client.
questions.explanation: Stakeholder analysis identifies and assesses all parties who contribute requirements or are affected by the system. Only identified stakeholders can be included in elicitation. Architecture alignment, budget planning, and communication channels are subsequent activities.

questions.prompt: A requirements team is creating a stakeholder map for a hospital information system. Which group is often overlooked but is critical to the system?
options: Doctors and nurses, who are obvious primary users.
Data-protection officers, IT operations, and billing departments—indirect stakeholders with binding requirements.
The software development team implementing the system.
The test team conducting acceptance testing.
questions.explanation: Direct users such as doctors and nurses are rarely missed. Indirect stakeholders—data-protection officers, IT operations, and billing departments—often are overlooked, yet they have binding requirements that are difficult to add later. Developers and testers are internal project roles.

questions.prompt: In a formal Fagan inspection, which role steers the process and ensures that every phase is completed correctly?
options: Author.
Moderator.
Scribe.
Inspector/reviewer.
questions.explanation: The moderator plans and leads the inspection, ensures correct role assignments, follows the phases, and manages time. The author created the document and does not moderate their own work; the scribe records defects; reviewers examine the content.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of defect density (defects per page) as an inspection metric?
options: It measures the performance of individual reviewers.
It identifies document sections with an above-average number of problems.
It proves that the document meets the minimum acceptance quality.
It predicts the duration of the next inspection.
questions.explanation: Defect density helps locate problem areas: sections with high density may have structural quality issues and need targeted rework. It does not measure reviewer performance, establish release criteria, or predict inspection duration.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is a typical REQUIREMENT ATTRIBUTE that should be assigned to each managed requirement?
options: The name of the developer who will implement it.
A priority value (for example, high/medium/low) indicating its relative value.
The estimated number of lines of code needed for implementation.
The planned deployment date of the first production release.
questions.explanation: Priority is a common requirement lifecycle attribute that expresses relative value or urgency and supports scope management. Other attributes include status, version, source, acceptance criteria, and risk. Developer names, code lines, and deployment dates are project or implementation data, not RE attributes.

questions.prompt: What does VERSIONING of requirements mean in requirements management?
options: Assigning version numbers only to distinguish product releases.
Systematically tracking all requirement changes so previous states can be understood and restored.
Freezing all requirements at the end of analysis to prevent changes.
Assigning a version number to a requirements document after its first CCB approval.
questions.explanation: Requirements versioning records changes over time, including who changed what, when, and why. This makes previous states reproducible and decisions traceable. It is not product release numbering, freezing requirements (a baseline), or merely numbering a document.

questions.prompt: A team needs to model data structures and their relationships in a warehouse-management system (product, supplier, order, storage location). Which notation is most suitable?
options: Activity diagram—shows the process flow of warehouse movements.
Sequence diagram—shows communication between the warehouse system and ERP.
Class diagram or entity-relationship diagram (ERD)—models static data structures and relationships.
State machine—models the states of a warehouse item.
questions.explanation: Class and ER diagrams are standard notations for static data structures: entities, attributes, and relationships. Activity diagrams show processes, sequence diagrams show communication, and state machines show object states. The question asks for structural, not behavioral, modeling.

questions.prompt: How does IREB define Requirements Engineering (RE) in its CPRE syllabus?
options: The technical implementation of software requirements by a development team.
A systems discipline concerned with eliciting, documenting, validating, and managing requirements for a system.
The preparation of a complete requirements specification before software development begins.
The project-management function that estimates software project costs.
questions.explanation: IREB defines RE as a systems discipline encompassing the activities needed to elicit, document, validate, and manage requirements. It is not limited to implementation, one document, or project management.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is NOT a quality criterion for an INDIVIDUAL requirement?
options: Testability—the requirement contains a measurable or verifiable threshold.
Unambiguity—the requirement has only one possible interpretation.
Specification consistency—all requirements in the document do not contradict one another.
Atomicity—the requirement describes exactly one property or capability.
questions.explanation: Specification consistency is a property of the document as a whole, not of an individual requirement. Individual requirement quality criteria include unambiguity, correctness, completeness, testability, atomicity, and understandability.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly describes VERIFICATION in requirements engineering?
options: Verification checks whether requirements meet actual stakeholder needs.
Verification checks whether the implementation conforms to the specification—‘Are we building the system RIGHT?’
Verification checks whether the system-context model is complete.
Verification checks whether all stakeholders have approved the requirements.
questions.explanation: Verification asks, ‘Are we building the system RIGHT?’—implementation versus specification. Validation asks, ‘Are we building the RIGHT system?’—specification versus stakeholder needs. Verification checks artifact-to-artifact consistency; validation checks relevance to the real world.

questions.prompt: What is the Scribe’s role in a formal inspection?
options: Lead the inspection process and coordinate all phases.
Explain the document under review to the reviewers.
Record defects and comments during the inspection meeting.
Prepare checklists for reviewers’ individual preparation.
questions.explanation: The Scribe records findings during the inspection meeting. The Moderator leads the process; the Author explains the document during the overview; checklists are typically supplied by the Moderator or standard process.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of a GLOSSARY in requirements engineering?
options: List all system functions in alphabetical order.
Define domain terms and abbreviations consistently to prevent ambiguity in requirements.
Document all approved requirement changes.
Describe the system architecture in language stakeholders can understand.
questions.explanation: A glossary gives project-specific terms clear, binding definitions and is a key tool against terminology ambiguity. For example, ‘customer’ could mean an end user, client, or external system. Without a glossary, stakeholders may interpret the same term differently.

questions.prompt: According to ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148, which modal verb marks an OPTIONAL requirement in English-language specifications?
options: shall
should
may
will
questions.explanation: ‘Shall’ means mandatory, ‘should’ means recommended but not required, and ‘may’ means optional. Choosing the correct modal verb has significant legal and technical consequences for a requirement’s binding force.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is NOT part of the SYSTEM CONTEXT?
options: An external payment-provider system that processes transactions.
The GDPR as a legal requirement for the system.
The internal database schema of the system being developed.
The organization’s data-protection officer as an indirect stakeholder.
questions.explanation: The internal database schema is a design decision inside the system boundary. The system context includes only elements outside that boundary: external systems, legal requirements, and stakeholders.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is NOT an IREB review type?
options: Walkthrough
Formal inspection (Fagan inspection)
Brainstorming
Technical review
questions.explanation: Brainstorming is an elicitation technique, not a review type. IREB review types include informal review, walkthrough, technical review, and formal inspection. Brainstorming generates requirements creatively rather than checking documents.

questions.prompt: A requirement says: ‘The system SHALL encrypt all passwords using AES-256.’ Which statement about its binding force is correct?
options: ‘Shall’ marks a recommendation, similar to ‘should’.
‘Shall’ marks a mandatory requirement—the implementation MUST use AES-256.
‘Shall’ and ‘should’ are equivalent in modern standards.
The requirement is invalid because ‘shall’ must not be used for security requirements.
questions.explanation: ‘Shall’ is the strongest normative keyword and indicates a mandatory requirement. ‘Should’ is recommended; ‘may’ is optional. Confusing ‘shall’ and ‘should’ is a common exam error with real contractual consequences.

questions.prompt: A system was fully implemented according to its specification. During acceptance testing, it becomes clear that the system does not solve the business problem. What happened?
options: A verification failure—the implementation does not conform to the specification.
A validation failure—the specification does not reflect actual stakeholder needs.
A verification failure—the specification does not reflect actual stakeholder needs.
A validation failure—the implementation does not conform to the specification.
questions.explanation: The implementation conforms to the specification, so verification succeeded. The specification failed to capture real needs, which is a validation failure. Option C swaps verification and validation; option D reverses cause and effect.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between a USE CASE and a USE-CASE SCENARIO?
options: A use case describes one specific path; a use-case scenario describes all possible paths.
A use case covers possible paths (main, alternative, and exception flows); a use-case scenario describes one specific path.
A use-case scenario is another name for a use-case diagram.
Developers create use cases; testers create use-case scenarios.
questions.explanation: A use case covers an application goal with its main flow, alternatives, and exceptions. A use-case scenario is one specific execution path, such as the main flow or one error case. Option A reverses the definitions.

questions.prompt: What are CONSTRAINTS in the IREB sense?
options: Requirements describing how well the system must perform its functions.
Prescribed restrictions that limit the solution space and cannot be changed through the RE process.
Requirements describing system behavior in exceptional situations.
Non-technical requirements that come exclusively from regulators.
questions.explanation: Constraints are given restrictions on the solution space, such as technology mandates, legal requirements, or budget limits. They are treated as given rather than negotiated through RE. Option A describes quality requirements; option C describes exceptional behavior.

questions.prompt: What is the main purpose of a GLOSSARY in requirements documentation?
options: List all use cases and their actors.
Define project-specific terms consistently to avoid ambiguity.
Present all quality requirements in a structured format.
List all stakeholders and their roles.
questions.explanation: A glossary standardizes the meaning of domain terms in a project. Stakeholders may use the same word differently; clear definitions prevent misunderstandings in requirements.

questions.prompt: A requirement states: ‘The system should be user-friendly.’ What is the primary quality problem?
options: It is redundant because it repeats an existing requirement.
It is not atomic because it contains several independent requirements.
It is not verifiable because ‘user-friendly’ is not a measurable criterion.
It is contradictory because it conflicts with typical performance requirements.
questions.explanation: ‘User-friendly’ is subjective and not measurable, so there is no objective test for satisfaction. A verifiable version might specify that task X can be completed in no more than three clicks.

questions.prompt: In a FORMAL INSPECTION (Fagan inspection), which role leads the inspection meeting?
options: The document’s author.
The reviewer.
The moderator (meeting leader).
The client.
questions.explanation: The moderator leads the Fagan inspection meeting and steers the discussion. The author must not moderate their own document because of the conflict of interest; the roles are deliberately separated.

questions.prompt: Why does IREB describe the requirements engineering process as ITERATIVE?
options: Because requirements engineering is used only in agile projects.
Because activities such as elicitation, documentation, and validation are repeated in cycles and refine one another.
Because exactly three iterations must be completed in every project.
Because stakeholders are not allowed to introduce new requirements during the project.
questions.explanation: Elicitation, documentation, and validation are repeated and refine one another rather than occurring once in a strict sequence. New findings during validation may lead to further elicitation. This cycle is intentional.

questions.prompt: What is the primary goal of NEGOTIATION in the IREB RE process?
options: Convince the client to accept all stakeholder requirements.
Resolve conflicting or competing stakeholder requirements and find an acceptable solution.
Prioritize requirements and assign them to releases.
Agree on technical feasibility with the development team.
questions.explanation: Negotiation aims to resolve conflicts between stakeholders. The result is an accepted priority or compromise. Prioritization is related but is a separate process activity.

questions.prompt: What is an RE ARTIFACT according to the IREB syllabus?
options: A document created exclusively by requirements engineers.
Any work product of the RE process, such as a requirements specification, use-case model, or glossary.
A software system developed as the result of the RE process.
A formal description of the system architecture.
questions.explanation: An RE artifact is any work product of the RE process. It may be a document, model, or supporting material. Artifacts are not created exclusively by requirements engineers; stakeholders and developers may contribute too.

questions.prompt: Compared with a USE-CASE DESCRIPTION, what does a USE-CASE DIAGRAM show?
options: The diagram describes detailed flows for all scenarios; the description gives only an overview.
The diagram gives a structural overview of use cases and actors; the description contains detailed flow steps.
The diagram and description contain the same information in different forms.
The diagram is normative; the description is informal and optional.
questions.explanation: A use-case diagram provides a structural overview of actors, use cases, and their relationships. Detailed main, alternative, and exception flows appear in the textual use-case description. Option A reverses their roles.

questions.prompt: An accountant performs daily work easily but cannot explain how: ‘I just do it.’ Which elicitation technique is most suitable?
options: Structured interview—the accountant can systematically describe the steps.
Prototyping—a click-through prototype helps the accountant articulate requirements.
Field observation (ethnography)—the requirements engineer observes the accountant at work.
Document analysis—existing manuals describe the correct workflows.
questions.explanation: The scenario involves tacit knowledge: the expert knows how to do the work but cannot verbalize it. Field observation is suitable because the requirements engineer directly observes the work rather than relying on a verbal account.

questions.prompt: A requirement says: ‘The system should respond quickly.’ Which revised wording best meets IREB’s verifiability criterion?
options: The system should respond as quickly as possible.
The system should have an acceptable response time.
The system shall respond to user input within 2 seconds.
The system should be performant and responsive.
questions.explanation: Only option C provides a measurable criterion (2 seconds) that can be verified in a performance test. ‘As quickly as possible’, ‘acceptable’, and ‘performant’ are subjective and not testable.

questions.prompt: Marketing demands ‘no login barrier—maximum reach.’ IT security demands ‘all users must authenticate.’ Which RE process step resolves this conflict?
options: Elicitation—interview more stakeholders to find consensus.
Documentation—record both requirements side by side in the specification.
Negotiation—facilitate resolution of the conflicting stakeholder requirements.
Validation—show the finished system and collect feedback.
questions.explanation: This is a stakeholder-interest conflict, the situation requirements negotiation is designed to address. The goal is an agreed solution, such as a guest mode with restricted access. Merely documenting both conflicting requirements does not resolve them.

questions.prompt: Which wording best follows the IREB sentence template for a MANDATORY SYSTEM FUNCTION?
options: It would be nice if the system could output reports in PDF format.
The system should be able to output reports in PDF format.
The system SHALL provide the function to output reports in PDF format.
The development team should implement a PDF export feature.
questions.explanation: The IREB template for mandatory system functions uses MUST/SHALL: system + SHALL + function. ‘Would be nice’ is optional; addressing the development team rather than the system is also incorrect.

questions.prompt: A team has a first draft of a requirements specification and wants quick, informal feedback without formal-process overhead. Which IREB review type is most suitable?
options: Formal inspection—maximum defect detection through a structured process.
Walkthrough—the author guides reviewers through the document and receives informal feedback.
Technical review—experts systematically check technical correctness.
Checklist-based peer review—a standardized check against predefined criteria.
questions.explanation: A walkthrough is the least formal review type: the author presents the document and reviewers discuss it without formal entry or exit criteria. It suits an early draft when quick feedback is desired.

questions.prompt: Fifty requirements must be prioritized with active stakeholder participation, but time is limited. Which method is most suitable?
options: Value analysis—precise but time-consuming.
Kano model—distinguishes basic, performance, and excitement attributes.
MoSCoW—classifies requirements as Must, Should, Could, or Won’t.
Complete pairwise comparison—compare every requirement with every other one.
questions.explanation: MoSCoW is quick to learn, participatory, and produces actionable priority groups. Pairwise comparison would require 1,225 comparisons for 50 requirements. Kano classifies customer-satisfaction attributes rather than implementation priorities.

questions.prompt: An order can be Open, Paid, or Cancelled. Open orders may become Paid or Cancelled; Paid orders cannot be cancelled. Which model best documents these rules?
options: Use-case diagram—shows actors and interactions.
Activity diagram—shows the chronological flow of order steps.
State diagram (statechart)—models states and permitted transitions.
Decision table—lists conditions and actions.
questions.explanation: State diagrams model an object’s defined states and transition rules. The scenario specifies discrete order states and restricted transitions.

questions.prompt: During perspective-based reading (PBR), reviewer Maria takes the tester perspective. What does she focus on?
options: Compatibility with the planned system architecture.
Clarity from the end user’s perspective.
Requirements that are not clearly testable or lack acceptance criteria.
Compliance with project budget constraints.
questions.explanation: The tester perspective focuses on testability, success criteria, and whether test cases can be derived. Architecture compatibility is the designer’s perspective; user comprehensibility is the end user’s perspective.

questions.prompt: A requirement says: ‘The system shall authenticate users, redirect them after successful login, and log failed logins.’ What quality problem is present?
options: Lack of unambiguity.
Lack of atomicity—the requirement should be split into separate requirements.
Lack of consistency with security standards.
Lack of completeness because exception handling is missing.
questions.explanation: The requirement combines authentication, redirecting after success, and logging failed logins. This violates atomicity. Split it into separate requirements that can be prioritized and tested independently.

questions.prompt: At the start of a hospital-administration software project, a stakeholder analysis is planned. What is the most sensible first step?
options: Invite everyone to a workshop to elicit requirements immediately.
Identify and categorize potential stakeholder groups, for example by direct or indirect influence.
Start documenting known requirements.
Immediately select and contact the most influential stakeholders.
questions.explanation: The first step is identification: determine who is affected, who has influence, and who has interests. Prioritization and invitations follow once the stakeholder landscape is known.

questions.prompt: What is the format of a USER STORY according to IREB?
options: As [function], the system shall deliver [benefit].
As [role], I want [goal/function] so that I receive [benefit].
As [stakeholder], I request [requirement] with [priority].
The system SHALL provide [function] for [role].
questions.explanation: The recognized format is ‘As [role], I want [goal/function], so that [benefit].’ It answers who, what, and why. The benefit clause explains value and helps the Product Owner prioritize.

questions.prompt: What are ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA for a user story?
options: Technical design constraints the development team must follow.
Conditions that must be met for a user story to be accepted as complete.
A priority list for implementing stories during a sprint.
Quality standards that apply to every story in the project.
questions.explanation: Acceptance criteria define when a user story is done. They are ideally written with the story and checked during the sprint review. Without them, there is no objective completion measure.

questions.prompt: What does the GIVEN-WHEN-THEN format describe?
options: A framework for prioritizing user stories in the Product Backlog.
A structure for acceptance criteria: precondition (Given), action (When), expected result (Then).
The role/goal/benefit user-story format.
A method for estimating story points.
questions.explanation: Given-When-Then structures acceptance criteria as testable scenarios: Given is the context or precondition, When is the triggering action, and Then is the expected result. It is distinct from the user-story format.

questions.prompt: What is a PRODUCT BACKLOG?
options: A fully elaborated requirements specification for the entire product.
A prioritized list of all known requirements, features, and improvements for the product.
A record of completed sprints and delivered features.
A technical implementation plan for the next sprint.
questions.explanation: The Product Backlog is the central requirements artifact in agile projects: a continuously maintained, prioritized list of requirements such as user stories, epics, bugs, and technical debt. The Product Owner is responsible for its content and prioritization.

questions.prompt: Which CORE FUNCTION does a REQUIREMENTS MANAGEMENT TOOL (RM tool) primarily support?
options: Automatic code generation from requirement text.
Managing, versioning, and tracing requirements.
Project scheduling and resource allocation.
Static code analysis and quality assurance.
questions.explanation: RM tools specialize in managing large sets of requirements, maintaining change history, traceability to tests/design/code, and status tracking. Code generation belongs to model-driven engineering; scheduling to project management; code analysis to development/DevOps.

questions.prompt: Which SCRUM EVENT most closely corresponds to the RE activity of VALIDATION?
options: Sprint Planning—requirements are decomposed into tasks.
Sprint Review—the team presents the completed increment to the Product Owner and stakeholders.
Daily Scrum—the team coordinates daily work.
Sprint Retrospective—the team reflects on its process.
questions.explanation: The Sprint Review is Scrum’s validation event: stakeholders inspect the completed increment against their expectations. Feedback may lead to new or changed backlog items. Planning, the daily scrum, and the retrospective serve different purposes.

questions.prompt: What does TRACEABILITY mean in requirements engineering?
options: The ability to rank requirements by priority.
The ability to trace each requirement back to its source and link it forward to artifacts such as tests, design, and code.
A measure of how understandable a requirements specification is.
The property that requirements can be reviewed without tool support.
questions.explanation: Traceability works in both directions: backward to a source such as a stakeholder or law, and forward to implementation, tests, and design. It supports impact analysis by identifying artifacts affected by a change.

questions.prompt: Which agile ARTIFACT most closely corresponds to a requirements specification?
options: The sprint burndown chart.
The prioritized Product Backlog with user stories and acceptance criteria.
The team velocity chart.
The release Gantt chart.
questions.explanation: In agile RE, the Product Backlog—with user stories, acceptance criteria, and supporting descriptions—acts as the living, prioritized requirements artifact. The other options support project monitoring and management.

questions.prompt: What does the SYSTEM CONTEXT include according to IREB?
options: Only the system’s direct end users.
All elements in the system environment that influence or are influenced by the system.
The system’s internal design, including all subsystems.
All stakeholders who participate in requirements reviews.
questions.explanation: The system context includes relevant elements outside the system boundary, such as neighboring systems, users, regulations, and the physical environment. Internal design decisions lie inside the system boundary.

questions.prompt: What does the SYSTEM BOUNDARY separate?
options: Functional from non-functional requirements.
The system being developed from its environment (context).
The project team from stakeholders.
Mandatory from optional requirements.
questions.explanation: The system boundary separates the system being developed from everything outside it. It defines what is built and what is part of the environment. Drawing this boundary is a key RE decision.

questions.prompt: What is a NEIGHBORING SYSTEM in the IREB sense?
options: A system from the same vendor with a shared codebase.
A system outside the system boundary that exchanges data or control signals with the system being developed.
A backup system activated if the main system fails.
A legacy system replaced by the new system.
questions.explanation: Neighboring systems are outside the system boundary and have direct interfaces with the system. They are relevant because they create interface requirements; they are treated as given, not developed as part of the system.

questions.prompt: What is IRRELEVANT SYSTEM CONTEXT?
options: Stakeholders who do not provide requirements.
Parts of the environment that neither influence nor are influenced by the system.
Requirements prioritized as ‘Could have’.
External systems with low integration effort.
questions.explanation: Irrelevant context consists of environmental elements that have no influence on the system and are not influenced by it. Delimiting the relevant context helps prevent scope creep.

questions.prompt: What does a CONTEXT DIAGRAM show?
options: The system’s internal classes and their relationships.
The system as a black box, relevant neighboring systems/actors, and data flows across the system boundary.
All system use cases and their actors.
The schedule for requirements elicitation workshops.
questions.explanation: A context diagram shows the system as a black box, relevant external systems and actors, and interfaces or data flows across the system boundary. It is an output of context analysis and supports requirements elicitation.

questions.prompt: Who is considered a STAKEHOLDER according to IREB?
options: Only people who use the system every day.
Any person, group, or organization that directly or indirectly influences requirements or is affected by the system.
Only the client and the development team.
Only people entitled to vote in requirements reviews.
questions.explanation: IREB uses a broad definition: stakeholders may have direct influence, such as users and clients, or indirect influence, such as regulators, data-protection officers, or affected third parties. Anyone who provides requirements or is affected by the system is a stakeholder, even if they do not use it.

questions.prompt: Which FOUR basic elements does a DATA FLOW DIAGRAM (DFD) contain?
options: Classes, attributes, methods, and inheritance relationships.
Processes, data stores, external entities, and data flows.
States, transitions, events, and actions.
Actors, use cases, include and extend relationships.
questions.explanation: The four DFD elements are processes that transform data, data stores, external entities that provide or receive data, and labeled data flows between elements.

questions.prompt: What does BPMN (Business Process Model and Notation) primarily model?
options: Data structures and their relationships within a system.
Business processes and workflows using events, gateways, and tasks.
Static classes and associations in an object model.
An object’s states and the events that trigger transitions.
questions.explanation: BPMN is a standard notation for business-process modeling: who does what and in what order. Its core elements include events, activities, gateways, and sequence flows. It models organizational workflow rather than data structure or system states.

questions.prompt: What is the function of a GATEWAY in a BPMN diagram?
options: It represents a task performed simultaneously by several participants.
It controls the flow by branching or synchronizing paths according to conditions or parallelism.
It marks the start or end of a process.
It shows an interface to an external system.
questions.explanation: BPMN gateways control process flow. XOR gateways choose a path, AND gateways split or synchronize parallel paths, and OR gateways select one or more paths. Events represent process start and end points.

questions.prompt: A team wants to model data movement among a system, database, and external interfaces. Which notation is most suitable?
options: BPMN—models business processes with events and gateways.
DFD (data flow diagram)—visualizes data flows, processes, data stores, and external entities.
State diagram—describes system state transitions.
Class diagram—shows data structures and relationships.
questions.explanation: DFDs are designed for data-flow modeling: where data comes from, how it is transformed, and where it is stored or sent. BPMN focuses on organizational workflow. For a technical data-flow perspective, a DFD is the suitable notation.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between DFD Level 0 and DFD Level 1?
options: Level 0 contains more detail than Level 1.
Level 0 shows the whole system as a single process; Level 1 decomposes it into subprocesses and data flows.
Level 0 contains internal data stores; Level 1 shows only external entities.
Both levels contain the same information in different layouts.
questions.explanation: DFDs are hierarchical. Level 0 (the context diagram) shows the system as one abstract process, with external entities and flows across the boundary. Level 1 decomposes that process into internal subprocesses and data stores.

questions.prompt: What does a LANE represent within a BPMN pool?
options: An optional process branch activated in exceptional cases.
A responsibility area within a process assigned to a role or department.
A parallel process running independently from the main process.
A database or external service accessed by the process.
questions.explanation: In BPMN, a pool represents a participant, such as an organization or system. Lanes divide a pool into responsibility areas, such as roles or departments, and show who performs each activity.

questions.prompt: What is the goal of REQUIREMENTS ENGINEERING (RE)?
options: Design the system’s technical architecture.
Elicit, document, validate, and manage requirements to create a shared understanding of the system.
Plan and execute software tests.
Create project plans and allocate resources.
questions.explanation: Requirements engineering systematically handles requirements through elicitation, documentation, validation, and management. Its goal is a shared, consistent understanding of the system to be built.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between ELICITATION and DOCUMENTATION in the RE process?
options: Elicitation is more formal than documentation.
Elicitation obtains requirements from stakeholders; documentation records them in artifacts.
Elicitation takes place after documentation.
Elicitation and documentation are synonyms for the same step.
questions.explanation: Elicitation obtains requirements from stakeholders, documents, and other sources. Documentation records the elicited requirements in structured artifacts such as specifications, user stories, or use-case descriptions. They are distinct but closely connected activities.

questions.prompt: What characterizes a STRUCTURED INTERVIEW?
options: The interviewer follows no set guide and freely adapts questions.
All questions are prepared in advance; every interviewee receives the same questions in the same order.
The interview ends only when all topics have been exhausted.
Structured interviews are conducted exclusively in writing.
questions.explanation: A structured interview uses a fixed questionnaire: all stakeholders receive the same questions, enabling direct comparison. Its disadvantage is limited tailoring. Unstructured interviews are open and flexible; semi-structured interviews combine both approaches.

questions.prompt: What does COMPLETENESS mean for an INDIVIDUAL requirement?
options: All necessary system requirements are present in the specification.
The requirement contains all information needed for implementation and testing.
The requirement has been approved by all stakeholders.
The requirement contains no unnecessary details.
questions.explanation: At the individual-requirement level, completeness means the requirement contains all information needed by a developer to implement it and by a tester to test it. Specification completeness—whether all necessary requirements are included—is a separate, higher-level property.

questions.prompt: What is the main difference between a REVIEW and a TEST in requirements verification?
options: Reviews are conducted only by external reviewers; tests by the internal team.
Reviews examine documents through human inspection; tests examine executable systems by running them.
Reviews are always cheaper than tests.
Reviews examine only functional requirements; tests only non-functional requirements.
questions.explanation: Reviews are static techniques: people inspect written artifacts without executing the system. Tests are dynamic: the system is run and its behavior checked. Requirements reviews can find defects before code is written, when correction is least costly.

questions.prompt: What is a BASELINE in requirements management?
options: The minimum number of requirements for a release.
An agreed and approved state of requirements against which changes are formally managed.
A document describing the system’s technical foundations.
The first production version of the system.
questions.explanation: A baseline is a formally agreed, versioned state of requirements. It marks a control point: subsequent changes are handled through the formal change process. It does not freeze requirements; changes remain possible but must be requested, analyzed, and approved.

questions.prompt: What is the BASIC PRINCIPLE of brainstorming as an elicitation technique?
options: Ideas are immediately evaluated and prioritized so only the best are pursued.
Ideas are first collected without criticism or evaluation during the idea-generation phase.
Each participant submits ideas in writing on a questionnaire.
Brainstorming is conducted only with individual experts.
questions.explanation: Brainstorming prioritizes quantity during the idea-generation phase. Criticism, disagreement, and evaluation are postponed because they can inhibit creativity. Ideas are structured and assessed after collection.

questions.prompt: What is the MAIN problem with requirements written only in NATURAL LANGUAGE?
options: They are too precise and leave no room for solutions.
Natural language is inherently ambiguous—readers may interpret terms differently.
They cannot be converted into use cases.
They are understandable only to technical stakeholders.
questions.explanation: Natural language is expressive but prone to ambiguity. For example, ‘the system shall be fast’ leaves unclear how fast, for whom, and under which conditions. Templates, glossaries, and models reduce ambiguity, while natural language remains widely used because stakeholders can understand it.

questions.prompt: What is the MAIN PURPOSE of a SENTENCE TEMPLATE (structured natural-language template) in requirements documentation?
options: Convert requirements into formal predicate logic.
Standardize the structure of natural-language requirements and reduce ambiguity.
Replace graphical models such as UML diagrams.
Set the priority of every requirement.
questions.explanation: A sentence template prescribes a consistent syntax, typically system + modal verb (MUST/SHOULD/MAY) + action and object. This reduces ambiguity and gives requirements a uniform format. Templates do not replace models or set priorities.

questions.prompt: A system function is OPTIONAL—the system may provide it but is not required to. Which modal verb is correct according to the IREB sentence template?
options: MUST—mandatory and strictly required.
SHOULD—strongly desired but may be omitted with justification.
MAY—optional; the system has discretion.
WILL—planned for the future but not yet decided.
questions.explanation: IREB distinguishes MUST (mandatory), SHOULD (strongly desired; deviations need justification), and MAY (optional). MAY is appropriate for a purely optional function. WILL is not an IREB modal verb.

questions.prompt: What is a CIRCULAR DEFINITION in a glossary?
options: A term is defined using a synonym that is not included in the glossary.
A term is defined using itself or another term that, in turn, uses the first term in its definition.
A term has more than one accepted domain definition.
A term is too broad and applies to multiple concepts.
questions.explanation: A circular definition goes in a circle: a term is explained using itself, or two terms define each other. Glossary definitions should not be circular or self-referential.

questions.prompt: Which glossary entry best follows IREB quality rules for glossaries?
