options: ‘User: someone who uses the system.’
‘Authentication: the process of verifying that a user is who they claim to be, for example by entering login credentials.’
‘Login: the process by which a user logs in.’
‘Session: an active user session in the system.’
questions.explanation: Option B defines authentication without relying on the term itself and describes its purpose and mechanism. Options A, C, and D are circular or essentially repeat the term rather than defining it.

questions.prompt: A requirement says: ‘The login button MUST be accessible to users with visual impairments (in accordance with WCAG 2.1 Level AA).’ Is this requirement VERIFIABLE?
options: No—‘accessible’ is subjective and has no numerical value.
Yes—WCAG 2.1 Level AA is a defined standard whose conformance can be checked as pass/fail.
No—accessibility can only be measured through user testing.
Yes, but only if a response time in milliseconds is also specified.
questions.explanation: Verifiability does not require a numerical measurement; a binary pass/fail check is sufficient. WCAG 2.1 AA defines specific criteria, and an audit can determine whether they are met. Verifiability is not the same as measurability.

questions.prompt: REQ-1: ‘User data MUST be deleted after 3 years (GDPR).’ REQ-2: ‘Booking data MUST be archived for 10 years (HGB).’ Both apply to the same records. What is the correct RE action?
options: GDPR takes precedence because data protection is more important than commercial law.
HGB takes precedence because retention obligations override deletion requirements.
Escalate the conflict to the relevant legal and compliance stakeholders; RE cannot resolve this legal conflict alone.
Document both requirements and let the development team decide.
questions.explanation: This is a genuine legal conflict between GDPR and commercial law that the requirements engineer cannot resolve independently. Document the conflict, identify the relevant legal, privacy, and compliance stakeholders, and escalate it to an authorized decision-maker.

questions.prompt: A medical device (FDA Class II) must be submitted for approval in two weeks. The project manager wants to skip the formal inspection and use an informal walkthrough to save time. As the RE lead, what should you do?
options: Agree—a walkthrough is an acceptable substitute for a formal inspection under time pressure.
Accept the walkthrough but also conduct a shortened checklist review.
Document the decision to omit the formal inspection and formally ensure that the project manager acknowledges responsibility for compliance risks.
Postpone the formal inspection until after submission.
questions.explanation: Formal inspection may be required by the quality-management system for regulated products. The RE lead should not approve an exception alone. Clearly communicate and document the risk and obtain a decision from the authorized responsible person; do not silently agree or postpone the review independently.

questions.prompt: REQ-A: ‘API calls MUST respond in under 100 ms.’ REQ-B: ‘Every call MUST undergo zero-trust validation.’ Both are prioritized, but the development team says they cannot be implemented together. What should RE do?
options: Relax the performance requirement to 500 ms because security always takes precedence.
Remove the zero-trust requirement because performance is more critical to user acceptance.
Record the conflict formally, invite the stakeholders to a moderated prioritization decision, and document the decision.
Allow the development team to choose a solution on its own.
questions.explanation: Two valid, prioritized requirements conflict technically. RE should not discard either unilaterally or delegate the decision to developers. Record the conflict, bring decision-authorized stakeholders together, moderate the discussion, and document the decision and its rationale.

questions.prompt: In sprint 8 of 10, a data-protection officer joins the project and identifies 12 new privacy requirements, three of which directly conflict with accepted requirements. The budget is exhausted. What is the CORRECT RE response?
options: Reject the 12 requirements because the budget does not allow changes.
Add all 12 immediately to the backlog and implement them in the next sprint.
Assess the new requirements, document conflicts with existing ones, evaluate risks, and agree on priorities with management.
Ask the data-protection officer to provide feedback only after project completion.
questions.explanation: Legitimate requirements, especially privacy requirements, should not simply be rejected or implemented without considering conflicts, cost, and risk. Capture them, document the conflicts, assess impacts, and obtain a management decision on priorities.

questions.prompt: Three stakeholders have disagreed about Feature X through three facilitated workshops. No agreement was reached, and no budget remains for further workshops. What is the NEXT RE action?
options: Remove Feature X from scope because unresolved conflicts block the project.
Adopt the majority position because two of the three stakeholders agree.
Use the escalation path: report the conflict and all positions to the project decision-maker or sponsor and request a binding decision.
Defer Feature X until after project completion and resubmit it as a change request.
questions.explanation: When facilitation does not achieve agreement, the decision belongs to the project authority or sponsor. RE should neutrally document positions, risks, and options, escalate the matter, and record the binding decision. Unilateral removal or majority voting is not an RE decision by default.

questions.prompt: An expert cannot verbalize their workflow: ‘I do it automatically.’ Both a structured interview and field observation seem plausible. According to IREB, which technique is MORE SUITABLE?
options: Structured interview—carefully worded questions help the expert explain their knowledge.
Field observation (ethnography)—the RE observes the work directly without relying on verbalization.
Both are equally suitable; it depends entirely on context.
Prototyping—a prototype helps the expert recognize their knowledge.
questions.explanation: An interview may help in some cases, but this scenario specifically says the expert cannot verbalize the knowledge. Field observation bypasses that barrier. For tacit knowledge that cannot be articulated, observation is the primary recommended technique.

questions.prompt: Two requirements logically contradict each other. Stakeholder A has higher priority than Stakeholder B. Does priority resolve the conflict?
options: Yes—the higher priority means A’s requirement applies and B’s is discarded.
Yes—prioritization is IREB’s standard mechanism for resolving conflicts.
No—priority determines implementation order, not logical contradictions. A content conflict requires negotiation or escalation.
No—logical contradictions cannot be resolved.
questions.explanation: Prioritization and conflict resolution are different RE activities. Priority addresses what to implement first; it does not remove a logical contradiction. Conflicting requirements must be negotiated or escalated to an authorized decision-maker.

questions.prompt: Data flows between subsystems need to be modeled. Both a DFD Level 0 and BPMN are possible. Which is more directly suitable for PURE DATA FLOWS?
options: BPMN—it is the ISO process standard and should always be preferred.
Data flow diagram (DFD)—it explicitly models data flows, data stores, and transformations without mixing in process-control logic.
Both are equivalent; the choice is purely conventional.
UML sequence diagram—it shows the timing of messages between components.
questions.explanation: BPMN is suited to business processes with control flow, gateways, events, and lanes. A DFD is more direct for showing which data flows where, what stores exist, and how data is transformed, without process-control detail.

questions.prompt: The GDPR requires the system being built to delete data after three years. Is the legislator (the EU Parliament) a STAKEHOLDER in the IREB sense?
options: No—stakeholders are only individuals or direct organizations that work with the system.
Yes—IREB includes any person or organization that provides or is affected by requirements, including legislators and regulators.
No—the legislator is an external influence but not a stakeholder.
Yes, but only if the legislator actively participates in the project.
questions.explanation: IREB defines stakeholders broadly as people, groups, or organizations with an interest in or influence on system requirements, or affected by them. Legislators and regulators provide requirements even if they do not participate in the project.

questions.prompt: User story: ‘As a user, I want the system to respond quickly so that I can work efficiently.’ Which INVEST criterion is most obviously violated?
options: I—Independent: the story depends on other stories.
N—Negotiable: the story is worded too rigidly.
T—Testable: ‘quickly’ is not measurable, so no acceptance criterion can be defined.
S—Small: the story is too large for a sprint.
questions.explanation: ‘Quickly’ is not testable. A measurable acceptance criterion such as a response time under a specified load cannot be derived from the story as written. This violates T (Testable) in INVEST.

questions.prompt: User story: ‘As a product manager, I want all features from the old software in the new system so that users do not have to relearn.’ Which INVEST criteria are violated?
options: Only I (Independent)—the story depends on the old software.
S (Small) and E (Estimable)—‘all features’ is unbounded and cannot be estimated.
Only T (Testable)—‘all features’ cannot be tested.
V (Valuable)—the benefit is unclear.
questions.explanation: ‘All features’ violates S (Small) because hundreds of features cannot fit into one sprint. It also violates E (Estimable), because the effort cannot be estimated without listing the features. This is an epic incorrectly written as one story; split it into smaller, estimable stories.

questions.prompt: Which user story follows the IREB format correctly AND best meets the INVEST criteria?
options: The system shall be able to export reports in PDF format.
As an accountant, I want to export monthly sales reports as PDFs so that I can forward them to the tax advisor.
As a user, I want to export all reports and statistics so that I can analyze data.
As an administrator, I want more control over the system.
questions.explanation: Option B specifies a clear role, concrete goal, and benefit. It is small enough, testable, independent, and estimable. A is not in user-story format; C is too broad and vague; D does not define a testable goal or benefit.

questions.prompt: Acceptance criterion for a login story: ‘Login MUST be secure and user-friendly.’ What is WRONG with it?
options: It is correct—‘secure’ and ‘user-friendly’ are accepted industry standards.
It violates INVEST’s T criterion—neither ‘secure’ nor ‘user-friendly’ is measurable or testable as written.
It is too short—acceptance criteria must contain at least three conditions.
It is acceptable as a high-level quality goal as long as technical details are left to the code.
questions.explanation: Acceptance criteria are tests, not wish lists. ‘Secure’ and ‘user-friendly’ are unoperationalized quality adjectives; a tester cannot objectively determine whether they are satisfied. Acceptance criteria must be concrete and testable.

questions.prompt: Which acceptance criterion correctly follows the GIVEN-WHEN-THEN format?
options: The system should lock the user after 3 failed attempts.
Given a registered user, when they enter 3 incorrect passwords, then their account is locked for 15 minutes.
When the user logs in, the system should respond securely.
The account is locked after failed attempts (details to follow).
questions.explanation: Given-When-Then specifies the initial context, trigger, and expected result. Option B clearly defines all three and is testable. The other options omit parts or remain vague.

questions.prompt: An accepted requirement is changed because of a new privacy rule. It had already been validated in reviews. What MUST happen after the change?
options: Nothing—a previously validated requirement remains valid even when changed.
The changed requirement MUST go through the review/validation process again.
Document the change; revalidation is optional depending on its scope.
Pass the change directly to implementation because a review already took place.
questions.explanation: A change invalidates previous reviews because the requirement now has different content. Change management and validation are linked: every content change requires revalidation, regardless of size, because even a small change can introduce defects or contradictions.

questions.prompt: A natural-language requirement says: ‘The system should be user-friendly.’ Which quality criterion is directly violated?
options: Completeness—important details are missing.
Consistency—the term ‘user-friendly’ contradicts other requirements.
Testability/verifiability—the requirement cannot be turned into a testable condition.
Unambiguity—the term is clear to every reader.
questions.explanation: ‘User-friendly’ is not verifiable as written because it has no measurable criterion or threshold. A sentence template alone is insufficient; the content must include testable acceptance criteria.

questions.prompt: A requirements team begins stakeholder interviews before defining the system context. What problem can result?
options: None—interviews provide all information needed to define the context.
The team may elicit requirements for out-of-scope elements or overlook relevant neighboring systems and influences.
The elicitation may be inefficient but is still substantively correct.
Prioritization is impossible without a system context.
questions.explanation: The system context establishes scope. Without it, the team may collect requirements for out-of-scope elements, miss neighboring systems, or misunderstand interfaces. Context analysis provides a framework for focused elicitation.

questions.prompt: After developer testing, the project manager says: ‘Validation is complete—the system has been tested.’ What is WRONG with this statement?
options: Nothing—successful tests complete validation in the IREB sense.
Tests check whether the system was built correctly (verification). RE validation checks whether the requirements reflect real stakeholder needs; tests alone cannot establish that.
Validation is optional if tests cover all requirements.
Validation occurs only at the beginning of the RE process.
questions.explanation: Tests primarily verify that implementation conforms to requirements. RE validation asks whether the requirements capture actual needs. It requires stakeholder feedback at the requirements level; even full test coverage cannot show that the requirements themselves were correct.

questions.prompt: An accepted requirement contradicts another (inconsistency). It was approved by stakeholders and recorded in the change log. What is the correct next step?
options: Remove the lower-quality requirement—consistency takes precedence over stakeholder acceptance.
Mark the contradiction as a known issue and continue.
Record a formal change request, involve both stakeholders in resolving the conflict, document the decision, and revalidate the corrected requirement.
Tell the development team and let them resolve the conflict in code.
questions.explanation: A quality defect in an accepted requirement is a change to an approved baseline and must be handled through change management. Involve stakeholders, document the resolution, and revalidate the corrected requirement. Deletion or delegation to developers bypasses required steps.

questions.prompt: IREB distinguishes several TYPES OF CONTEXT ELEMENTS. Which classification is correct?
options: Functional, non-functional, and constraint requirements.
People/roles, neighboring systems, processes and events, and where relevant physical objects/devices.
Input systems, output systems, and bidirectional systems.
Direct stakeholders, indirect stakeholders, and external regulators.
questions.explanation: IREB classifies context elements by nature: people and roles, neighboring systems, processes and events, and sometimes physical objects or devices. These categories help ensure that relevant context is not overlooked.

questions.prompt: The project team is debating whether an existing legacy payment system belongs inside the system boundary or should be treated as a neighboring system. Which criterion is decisive?
options: The payment system’s technical complexity—complex systems belong outside.
Whether the project team will develop, change, or control the payment system as part of the project.
The number of interfaces—more than three means it is a neighboring system.
Its cost—systems that incur costs remain outside the boundary.
questions.explanation: The decisive criterion is project scope and control: elements the team will develop or change are inside the boundary; given elements that will not be changed remain outside in the context. The boundary decision is an important early RE decision.

questions.prompt: A barcode scanner sends product IDs to an inventory-management system. How should it be classified in the system-context model?
options: As a neighboring system—it communicates through a defined interface.
As a human actor—an employee operates the scanner.
As a physical context element/device—an external technical device that supplies data.
As part of the system—the scanner is hardware belonging to the overall system.
questions.explanation: A barcode scanner is a physical device in the system context, not an IT system with its own logic or a human actor. It supplies data through an interface. Physical devices may create different interface requirements than systems or people.

questions.prompt: Which notation is IREB’s PRIMARY technique for showing the system context at the highest level of abstraction?
options: UML class diagram—models static data structures.
Context diagram (DFD Level 0)—shows the system as a black box, external entities, and data flows across the boundary.
UML sequence diagram—shows the timing of messages between components.
BPMN process diagram—shows business workflows.
questions.explanation: A context diagram, often represented as a Level-0 DFD, is a central technique for modeling system context. It shows the system as one undifferentiated black box, external entities outside it, and data flows or interactions across the boundary.

questions.prompt: What is the fundamental difference between a CONTEXT DIAGRAM and a UML USE-CASE DIAGRAM?
options: A context diagram shows individual system functions; a use-case diagram shows data flows.
A context diagram shows data flows and boundaries without functional detail; a use-case diagram shows which actors use which system functions.
They show the same thing and are interchangeable.
A use-case diagram contains internal system components; a context diagram does not.
questions.explanation: A context diagram shows external entities and flows across the system boundary without naming system functions. A use-case diagram shows the system’s functions and which actors use them. The diagrams complement each other: context scope overview versus functional overview.

questions.prompt: An arrow from ‘Tax authority’ to the system appears in a context diagram. What does the arrow correctly represent?
options: The tax authority is an internal project stakeholder.
An interface or influence crossing the system boundary, such as a reporting obligation or data-format requirement.
The arrow is wrong—government agencies never belong in context diagrams.
The tax authority has access rights to the system.
questions.explanation: In a context diagram, an arrow represents an interface, interaction, data flow, or influence crossing the system boundary. Government agencies may provide data, receive reports, or impose regulatory requirements and are valid external entities.

questions.prompt: Besides title and text, which STANDARD ATTRIBUTES should a complete requirement in a professional RE tool typically contain?
options: Only ID and priority; all other information belongs in the description.
ID, status, priority, author, source, version, stability, and possibly risk and effort estimate.
Only ID, date, and approval status; everything else is project-specific.
ID, category, and test implementation; all other attributes are optional.
questions.explanation: Common requirement attributes include a unique ID, lifecycle status, priority, author, source, version, stability, and sometimes risk and effort. They support filtering, reporting, and planning.

questions.prompt: How does a requirement’s STATUS typically change during a project?
options: It never changes; it is set once when the requirement is created.
It follows a lifecycle, such as proposed, under review, approved, implemented, tested, and accepted, with possible rejection or withdrawal along the way.
It only indicates whether the requirement was approved or rejected.
Only the client sets status; the RE team does not change it.
questions.explanation: Status is a dynamic lifecycle attribute. It tracks a requirement from submission through review and approval to implementation, testing, and acceptance, or rejection/withdrawal. Status transitions support progress tracking and coverage reporting.

questions.prompt: How are REQUIREMENT ATTRIBUTES practically useful in project management?
options: Only for final documentation; they have no use during development.
For filtering, progress reporting, risk analysis, and release planning.
Only to satisfy formal process requirements, with no practical benefit.
Only for external auditors; internal teams use other tracking methods.
questions.explanation: Attributes enable practical management: filter by status to find open requirements, by priority to focus resources, use stability to flag likely changes, and use source for stakeholder reporting. Effort and priority support release planning.

questions.prompt: When should a new BASELINE typically be created?
options: After every individual requirement change.
At defined project milestones, such as after elicitation, before system testing, or before a release.
Only at the beginning of the project; one baseline is sufficient for the entire project.
Only when the client approves a change.
questions.explanation: Baselines are established at phase boundaries or decision points, such as after elicitation, before system testing, or before a release. Creating one after every change is impractical; having only one may limit traceability and rollback options.

questions.prompt: A project has three baselines: B1 (development start), B2 (test start), and B3 (release candidate). Testing finds critical defects caused by faulty requirements in B3. What is the benefit of the earlier baselines?
options: Earlier baselines are useless once B3 exists.
B1 and B2 can be compared to determine when the problematic requirements were introduced and, if needed, restore an earlier state.
Earlier baselines matter only for external audits, not ongoing development.
Only B2 matters because B1 is too old.
questions.explanation: Baselines support recovery and comparison. Comparing B1, B2, and B3 can reveal when a faulty change was introduced, help locate the cause, and allow the team to return to a known earlier state rather than reconstructing the document from scratch.

questions.prompt: What is PAIRWISE COMPARISON as a prioritization technique, and what is its main limitation?
options: Stakeholders name their favorites; the limitation is subjectivity.
Each requirement is compared with every other requirement to create a relative ranking. The number of pairs grows as n×(n−1)/2, making it impractical for large sets.
Pairs of stakeholders discuss requirements; the limitation is time.
A game-theory method that requires numerical values.
questions.explanation: Pairwise comparison establishes preferences by comparing requirements two at a time. Its effort grows quadratically: 50 requirements require 1,225 comparisons. It can suit small sets but is impractical for large ones, where MoSCoW or weighted scoring may be more efficient.

questions.prompt: What is the BASIC PRINCIPLE of weighted scoring as a prioritization technique?
options: Rank requirements by a single criterion, such as user importance.
Rate each requirement against several weighted criteria, then combine the weighted scores into an overall ranking.
Divide requirements into two categories based only on implementation effort.
Let stakeholders vote anonymously and use the majority order.
questions.explanation: Weighted scoring makes multiple criteria explicit, such as customer value, risk, and effort. The weighted scores are combined into a total score. Its strength is transparency; its drawback is the effort required to create and maintain the scoring matrix.

questions.prompt: A team must prioritize 80 requirements with five stakeholders, three days available, diverse interests, and no clear majority. Which method is most suitable?
options: Pairwise comparison—it gives the most precise ranking.
Kano model—it classifies customer-satisfaction effects.
MoSCoW in a facilitated stakeholder session—it is quick, participatory, and produces actionable scope decisions.
Weighted scoring—its mathematical precision resolves diverse stakeholder interests.
questions.explanation: Pairwise comparison would require 3,160 comparisons, and scoring 80 requirements against several criteria with five stakeholders may exceed the budget. Kano classifies attributes but does not produce a release-priority ranking. MoSCoW is a pragmatic, transparent, participatory compromise that feeds into release planning.

questions.prompt: After sprint 4, the market changes when a competitor launches a similar product. What should the RE team do about prioritization?
options: Nothing—priorities are set only once at project start.
Review and, if needed, adjust priorities; features that differentiate the product may become more important. Prioritization is ongoing.
Change priorities only after the client submits a formal change request.
Restart prioritization from scratch because external changes invalidate all previous decisions.
questions.explanation: Prioritization should respond to market changes, competition, regulation, and stakeholder priorities. Existing rankings remain the basis until deliberately adjusted; they need not be discarded wholesale.

questions.prompt: What are ENTRY CRITERIA for a formal inspection?
options: Conditions that must be met after the inspection before the document is released.
Conditions that must be met before the inspection starts, such as a stable document version, reviewer preparation time, and available checklists.
A list of requirements to be examined during the inspection.
The client’s formal approval to conduct the inspection.
questions.explanation: Entry criteria protect inspection quality. Typical criteria include a stable document version, sufficient reviewer preparation time, available checklists and review materials, and an available moderator. If criteria are not met, the inspection should be postponed.

questions.prompt: What are EXIT CRITERIA for a formal inspection?
options: The maximum number of defects an inspection may find.
Conditions required for the inspection to be considered complete, such as recorded findings, assigned rework, and planned follow-up.
A list of reviewers who have completed their examination.
The date when results are sent to the client.
questions.explanation: Exit criteria ensure a defined conclusion with no loose ends. Typical criteria include recording and classifying all findings, assigning rework, and deciding whether reinspection is needed. The inspection is complete only after these conditions are met.

questions.prompt: Shortly before a planned inspection, a reviewer says: ‘I had no time for individual preparation; I have not read the document yet.’ What should the moderator do?
options: Start anyway; spontaneous feedback is valuable.
Postpone the inspection because required preparation was not completed and inspection quality is at risk.
Replace the reviewer immediately with someone else.
Extend the meeting so the reviewer can prepare during it.
questions.explanation: Individual preparation is a required phase and an entry criterion of a formal inspection. Without it, reviewers cannot contribute well-founded findings. The moderator should postpone until the entry criteria are met; spontaneous feedback is characteristic of a walkthrough, not a formal inspection.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between a MAJOR defect and a MINOR defect in an inspection?
options: Major means many words must be changed; minor means only one word.
A major defect prevents the document from serving as a development baseline and must be fixed first; a minor defect does not block the process.
Major defects are reported by clients; minor defects are found internally.
The distinction is project-specific; IREB gives no definition.
questions.explanation: Defect severity determines process consequences. A major defect makes the document unsuitable as a baseline until corrected, potentially requiring reinspection. A minor defect can be handled in follow-up without blocking continued work. The classification is made by the moderator with the team.

questions.prompt: A formal inspection records 12 findings: 3 major and 9 minor. The author revises the document. What happens during FOLLOW-UP?
options: Repeat the entire inspection because findings were found.
The moderator or a delegated reviewer checks that findings, especially major ones, were correctly addressed; if so, the document can be released.
The client reviews the revisions and releases the document.
All reviewers meet again for a complete reinspection of the revised document.
questions.explanation: Follow-up verifies the rework; it is not automatically a full reinspection. The moderator or delegate checks whether findings were addressed correctly. Reinspection is needed only if major defects remain or new serious issues are found.

questions.prompt: Besides reviews and prototyping, which VALIDATION TECHNIQUES does IREB mention?
options: Code review, unit testing, and integration testing.
Simulation, perspective-based reading (PBR), acceptance tests, and formal methods.
Brainstorming, mind mapping, and storyboarding.
Data-flow analysis, state-space analysis, and model checking.
questions.explanation: IREB validation techniques include reviews, prototyping, simulation, perspective-based reading, formal methods, and acceptance-test workshops. Code reviews and unit tests are verification techniques, not requirements validation techniques.

questions.prompt: What is PERSPECTIVE-BASED READING (PBR)?
options: A technique where a reviewer reads the document repeatedly from different viewpoints.
A review technique where each reviewer adopts a defined stakeholder perspective (such as tester, developer, or user) to find perspective-specific defect types.
A technique where the author revises the document from the client’s perspective.
An informal feedback method where stakeholders annotate the document themselves.
questions.explanation: PBR structures reviews by assigning reviewers specific roles. A tester looks for untestable requirements, a developer for incomplete technical specifications, and a user for usability issues. Different perspectives reveal different defect classes.

questions.prompt: A real-time system with complex behavior must be validated, but stakeholders find it difficult to mentally simulate the system. Which validation technique is particularly suitable?
options: Formal inspection—its high defect-detection rate always makes it the best choice.
Glossary-based review—consistent terminology is the foundation of all validation.
Simulation—a dynamic model lets stakeholders experience behavior and identify deviations from expectations.
Walkthrough—the author explains the behavior and stakeholders give feedback.
questions.explanation: Simulation is valuable for time-dependent or complex behavior that stakeholders cannot easily infer from specification text. Interactive what-if scenarios help them recognize deviations from expectations.

questions.prompt: An RE team has three weeks and two reviewers. It must ensure both requirement CORRECTNESS and AGREEMENT with stakeholder expectations. Which technique combination is most efficient?
options: Two complete Fagan inspections—one for correctness and one for stakeholder expectations.
A technical review for correctness combined with a prototype walkthrough with stakeholders to validate expectations.
Only informal reviews—nothing more is possible with two people and three weeks.
Only prototyping—stakeholder feedback matters more than correctness.
questions.explanation: A technical review uses reviewer expertise to check correctness; a prototype walkthrough directly validates stakeholder expectations. This targets two different review objectives without the capacity demands of two full formal inspections.

questions.prompt: Which SIX quality criteria does IREB specify for an INDIVIDUAL requirement?
options: Completeness, consistency, currency, traceability, unambiguity, testability.
Unambiguity, correctness, completeness, consistency, testability, and atomicity.
Testability, atomicity, modelability, unambiguity, relevance, and feasibility.
Correctness, completeness, atomicity, priority, testability, and readability.
questions.explanation: The six criteria are unambiguity, correctness, completeness, consistency, testability, and atomicity. They apply to individual requirements and should be assessed systematically.

questions.prompt: Which requirement best satisfies the IREB quality criteria?
options: The system should be performant, secure, and stable.
The system MUST respond to search queries within 1.5 seconds for 95% of requests under a standard load of 500 concurrent users.
The system should process user requests as quickly as possible.
The system MUST meet all security standards, redirect after login, and write logs.
questions.explanation: Option B defines measurable thresholds, a test context, and a load condition. It is unambiguous, atomic, sufficiently complete, and testable. A is vague and bundles attributes; C is vague; D bundles functions and refers to unspecified standards.

questions.prompt: Why is ATOMICITY a PREREQUISITE for TESTABILITY?
options: It is not a prerequisite; the two criteria are completely independent.
A non-atomic requirement combines properties, making it unclear which one failed when a test fails; mixing them undermines isolated testing.
Atomicity improves readability but does not affect testability.
An atomic requirement is automatically testable; the criteria always occur together.
questions.explanation: For ‘The system should be fast and secure,’ a failed test does not reveal which property failed. Atomicity is necessary for isolated testing, though it is not sufficient: an atomic requirement such as ‘the system should be fast’ may still be untestable.

questions.prompt: A requirement says: ‘The system should respond immediately to user input and log all user actions in an audit file.’ Which revision is FULLY CORRECT?
options: The system should respond immediately and completely to user input.
The system MUST process user input within 500 ms. Separately: The system MUST record every user action with a timestamp in the audit log.
The system should respond quickly to input and write logs.
The system MUST process, log, and confirm all actions within 500 ms.
questions.explanation: Option B fixes both problems: it splits the non-atomic requirement into two independent requirements and replaces the untestable ‘immediately’ with a measurable 500 ms threshold. The other options remain vague or bundle multiple aspects.

questions.prompt: An RE team reviews a specification containing 80 requirements. What is the most efficient systematic approach?
options: Rewrite each requirement completely as soon as a problem is found.
First check all requirements for atomicity, then testability and unambiguity, and finally compare them pairwise for consistency.
Check only the highest-priority requirements and skip the rest.
Start with consistency because contradictions are the most common problem.
questions.explanation: Use a logical funnel: check atomicity first because it is a structural prerequisite; then assess individual wording for testability and unambiguity; finally check consistency across requirements, a pairwise task with higher effort. This is most effective after individual requirements are cleaned up.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between COMPLETENESS of an INDIVIDUAL requirement and COMPLETENESS of a SPECIFICATION?
options: There is no difference; both mean the same thing.

Individual completeness means the requirement contains all information needed for implementation and testing; specification completeness means all necessary system requirements are present in the document.
Specification completeness means all requirements are atomic.
Individual completeness means the requirement has been approved by all stakeholders.
questions.explanation: These are different levels. Individual completeness asks whether this requirement contains all needed information. Specification completeness asks whether the document includes all necessary system requirements. A specification may contain complete individual requirements and still omit necessary requirements.

questions.prompt: REQ-3: ‘Load time MUST be under 2 seconds.’ REQ-7: ‘The system MUST identify the device, load preferences, and render content.’ In what order should quality assurance proceed?
options: Check REQ-3 first because performance requirements are more critical than functional ones.
First split REQ-7 because it combines three functions; then check the resulting atomic requirements for consistency with REQ-3, including possible impact of loading preferences on response time.
REQ-7 is correctly written; multiple actions in one request do not violate atomicity.
Both requirements are correct; no action is needed.
questions.explanation: REQ-7 combines device identification, preference loading, and rendering, so it violates atomicity. Split it first; then check dependencies and consistency with the load-time requirement, especially whether preference loading affects performance.

questions.prompt: A reviewer says: ‘This requirement is complete—I checked all six individual-requirement quality criteria, and it passes them all.’ Could the specification still be incomplete?
options: No—if every individual requirement passes the six criteria, the specification is automatically complete.
Yes—individual-requirement completeness and specification completeness are different quality dimensions. The specification may still omit necessary requirements.
No—a specification is complete by definition once approved.
Yes, but only if fewer than 90% of expected requirements are documented.
questions.explanation: Individual completeness asks whether this requirement has all information needed for implementation and testing. Specification completeness asks whether all necessary system requirements are included. A specification can contain perfectly written requirements and still omit others.

questions.prompt: What does the MAIN SUCCESS SCENARIO in a use-case description describe?
options: All possible errors and exceptions that may occur.
The optimal, error-free sequence of actor-system interactions that achieves the use case’s goal.
The preconditions that must be met before the use case.
All actors allowed to trigger the use case.
questions.explanation: The main success scenario describes step by step how the interaction proceeds when everything goes as planned, without errors or special cases. Errors and exceptions belong in alternative flows.

questions.prompt: What does the PRECONDITION of a use case define?
options: What the actor has achieved after the use case completes.
The system state or conditions that must hold BEFORE the use case starts.
Errors that may occur during the use case.
Interfaces between the use case and other use cases.
questions.explanation: A precondition defines the required starting state, such as ‘the user is logged in’ or ‘the shopping cart is not empty.’ If it is not met, the use case cannot start. It helps define scope and prepare test conditions.

questions.prompt: What does the POSTCONDITION of a use case define according to IREB?
options: Error states that may follow a failed use case.
The system state after the use case completes successfully.
The next action the actor should perform.
Technical requirements that must be met after implementation.
questions.explanation: The postcondition describes the guaranteed system state after successful completion, such as an order being stored and a confirmation email sent. It provides a testable definition of success; error states belong in alternative flows.

questions.prompt: Use case ‘Buy product’ has this main-flow step: ‘Step 4: The system processes the payment.’ What should an alternative flow for Step 4 document?
options: Nothing—alternative flows are optional and only needed for safety-critical systems.
What happens if payment fails, including the system response and the actor’s next action.
The name of the programmer who implements Step 4.
The payment component’s internal processing logic.
questions.explanation: Alternative flows describe deviations from the main flow, such as errors or special conditions. For a declined card, document the system response and possible next actor actions, such as trying another method or cancelling.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between STRUCTURAL MODELS and BEHAVIORAL MODELS in requirements documentation?
options: Structural models show time sequences; behavioral models show static data structures.
Structural models show WHAT exists (entities, attributes, relationships); behavioral models show HOW the system responds to events (flows, states, interactions).
Structural models are always UML; behavioral models are always textual.
Structural models are for developers; behavioral models are for stakeholders.
questions.explanation: Structural models, such as class diagrams and ERDs, describe the static ‘what’: entities, attributes, and relationships. Behavioral models, such as activity, state-machine, and sequence diagrams, describe the dynamic ‘how’: responses to events, order, and states. Both views support complete requirements.

questions.prompt: The team wants to document order states and the conditions for transitions. A developer suggests a class diagram. Is that correct?
options: Yes—class diagrams show every property of an entity, including its states.
No—a state machine diagram is suitable. Class diagrams show static structure, not dynamic state transitions.
Yes—a class diagram with a ‘status’ attribute is sufficient.
No—BPMN must always be used for state transitions.
questions.explanation: A class diagram can show a status attribute, but not which transitions are allowed, their triggering conditions, or associated actions. A state machine models discrete states and transitions. The two diagrams complement each other: structure versus behavior.

questions.prompt: An RE team needs a model for a workshop with business stakeholders who have no technical training. Which notation is most suitable?
options: UML sequence diagram—it precisely shows when messages are exchanged.
UML class diagram with multiplicities and association names.
BPMN process diagram or use-case diagram—both are more intuitive for business stakeholders without UML training.
Entity-relationship diagram—domain-independent and easy for everyone to understand.
questions.explanation: Models for business stakeholders should be understandable without specialized training. BPMN communicates business processes; use-case diagrams show system functions from a user perspective. Notation should fit the audience, not just maximize technical precision.

questions.prompt: When should a TEXTUAL DESCRIPTION (natural language) be preferred over a model?
options: Always—natural language is understandable to all stakeholders.
For simple, linear requirements without complex logic, and for diverse stakeholder groups unfamiliar with model notation.
When describing complex state transitions or data flows.
Textual descriptions are fully replaced by models; IREB recommends models only.
questions.explanation: Text is suitable for simple requirements, diverse audiences without modeling knowledge, and situations requiring quick documentation. Models are often better for complex branching flows, data structures, or state logic. IREB recommends a pragmatic mix; no notation is universally best.

questions.prompt: What is a DECISION TABLE suitable for in requirements documentation?
options: Documenting the chronological sequence of system events.
Systematically documenting combinations of input conditions and their corresponding system responses.
Visualizing data flows among internal system components.
Describing class structure and inheritance hierarchies.
questions.explanation: Decision tables suit complex conditional logic by listing combinations of conditions and corresponding actions. They help ensure that all combinations are considered, for example in tax calculations, authorization rules, or pricing logic.

questions.prompt: Order process: three user roles, eight branches, and four external systems. A stakeholder presentation is due in four weeks, with limited time and budget. Which documentation strategy is best?
options: Use only natural-language requirements because they are quickest to create and everyone understands them.
Use only use-case diagrams and BPMN for the presentation, without textual detail.
Combine BPMN for the process overview, use-case descriptions for the three most critical flows, and a glossary for the roles and external systems.
Create a complete formal UML specification with sequence diagrams for all eight branches.
questions.explanation: The complexity requires models, while time pressure rules out a full formal specification. BPMN communicates the process, textual use cases clarify critical flows, and a glossary aligns terminology. Diagrams alone may omit flow details and exceptions.

questions.prompt: During a requirements review, a stakeholder says: ‘This requirement does not describe what we really need.’ Which RE activity is triggered IMMEDIATELY?
options: Management—the requirement is entered in the change log.
Elicitation—the stakeholder’s actual needs are investigated again.
Documentation—the requirement is rewritten in a new template.
Negotiation—the stakeholder and team agree on wording.
questions.explanation: The review (validation) has revealed that the documented requirement does not reflect the real need. The next step is renewed elicitation, not merely rewriting the text. This is a feedback loop in the iterative RE process.

questions.prompt: During documentation, the RE team discovers that an important system function was never documented and no stakeholder mentioned it. What is the CORRECT next step?
options: Fill the gap using plausible assumptions and document them.
Return to elicitation and clarify the missing information with relevant stakeholders.
Finish the specification without it and add it later.
Begin development with existing requirements and resolve the gap in the sprint review.
questions.explanation: Documentation can reveal gaps that require renewed elicitation. Plausible assumptions are not a substitute for stakeholder-based requirements. Starting implementation without clarification shifts the problem and increases the risk of costly rework.

questions.prompt: A team hands requirements to development after elicitation and documentation, without validation. At acceptance testing, the client rejects 35% of the features. Which RE failure occurred?
options: Elicitation failure—too few stakeholders were interviewed.
Validation failure—the specification was never checked against actual stakeholder needs.
Verification failure—the implementation does not match the specification.
Management failure—change requests were not recorded correctly.
questions.explanation: The system may have been implemented according to the specification, so the problem is not necessarily verification. The specification did not reflect actual needs: a validation failure. Early stakeholder validation could have exposed the mismatch before correction became expensive.

questions.prompt: A WATERFALL project has a dedicated ‘RE phase’ at the beginning. Does this mean RE activities stop for the rest of the project?
options: Yes—requirements are frozen after the RE phase, so RE is complete.
No—requirements management and occasional further elicitation continue throughout the project.
Yes—RE activities after that phase violate the waterfall approach.
No—all four RE activities must be performed equally in every project phase.
questions.explanation: RE does not end with an initial phase. Once requirements exist, management and change control begin; changes may arise from technical findings, stakeholder feedback, or external events. The intensity and focus may vary, but RE continues throughout the project.

questions.prompt: In a SCRUM project, which events and activities correspond to IREB’s core RE activities?
options: RE takes place only during Sprint Planning.
Backlog Refinement corresponds roughly to elicitation and documentation; Sprint Review to validation; the Product Backlog to management.
RE is entirely the responsibility of the Scrum Master.
RE activities occur only at the beginning of each sprint.
questions.explanation: In Scrum, RE activities are distributed: Backlog Refinement elicits and documents stories and acceptance criteria; Sprint Review validates the increment with stakeholders; and the prioritized Product Backlog supports requirements management.

questions.prompt: In sprint 5 of 8, the project manager says: ‘RE is finished—we are only doing development now.’ What is WRONG with this statement?
options: Nothing—after the RE phase, the development team takes full responsibility.
Requirements management, traceability maintenance, and reprioritization continue through project completion; new or changed requirements still trigger RE activities.
RE is not finished in sprint 5; it ends with sprint 8.
RE ends only at production acceptance, not during the sprint.
questions.explanation: RE is a continuous cross-cutting activity, not a phase that simply ends. Change requests, review feedback, and new findings continue to trigger RE activities. Requirements management and traceability remain active throughout.

questions.prompt: The test team asks: ‘Which RE artifact should we use as the basis for deriving test cases?’ What is the CORRECT answer?
options: The system-architecture document created by development.
The requirements specification (SRS), the central RE artifact describing what the system MUST do.
Test cases should be derived independently from source code.
User acceptance test scripts supplied by the client.
questions.explanation: The requirements specification is the primary basis for test cases. Each documented requirement must be verifiable. Traceability links requirements to test cases; architecture describes how the system is built, while requirements describe what it must do.

questions.prompt: An audit finds GDPR violations in the requirements specification during a sprint. The sprint goal is due Monday. What is the correct RE response?
options: Address the findings after the sprint; the deadline is not yet critical.
Edit the specification immediately and abandon the sprint goal.
Record the findings as change requests, analyze impact, and escalate the sprint/compliance trade-off to the Product Owner without changing the baseline unilaterally.
Cancel the sprint immediately and schedule a compliance sprint.
questions.explanation: RE should not decide alone to cancel a sprint or alter a baseline. Formally record the compliance findings, analyze their impact, and escalate the decision to the Product Owner or authorized authority. Preserve baseline integrity until approval.

questions.prompt: A medical device calculates patient dosages with required accuracy of ≤0.01%. The budget allows exactly TWO validation techniques. Which combination has the highest priority?
options: Workshop with nurses + simulation.
Workshop with nurses + formal proof.
Formal proof + simulation using a regulatorily validated model.
Walkthrough + formal proof.
questions.explanation: Patient safety is the highest risk. Formal proof can establish the required accuracy mathematically; simulation complements it by evaluating behavior such as response time and fault tolerance. A stakeholder workshop is valuable but secondary to these two techniques for the stated accuracy goal.

questions.prompt: A calculation rule must be approved by the business department and directly implemented by development. The budget allows only ONE documentation artifact. Which model suits both purposes?
options: UML class diagram.
Natural-language requirement description.
Decision table.
BPMN process diagram.
questions.explanation: A decision table can be validated by business experts because each row represents a condition combination, and it can be implemented directly. Natural language may be ambiguous for implementation; BPMN models process flow rather than calculation logic.

questions.prompt: Machine operators cannot verbalize their work (tacit knowledge). There is no existing system or documentation. The budget allows TWO elicitation techniques. Which combination is appropriate?
options: Structured interview + document analysis.
Field observation + low-fidelity prototyping.
Workshop + questionnaire.
Contextual inquiry + formal expert interview.
questions.explanation: Tacit knowledge limits language-based techniques. Field observation directly captures work practices, and without an existing system a paper prototype lets stakeholders react to a concrete representation. Interview-based alternatives still rely on verbalization.

questions.prompt: REQ-47 (availability ≥99.9%) is in baseline B2. A stakeholder requests reducing it to 95%, but customer SLAs specify 99.9%. The CCB meets in five days. What should RE do TODAY?
options: Reject the change because it violates the SLA; RE makes that decision.
Temporarily enter the change in the specification as ‘Pending CCB.’
Record a change request and provide an impact analysis while leaving the baseline unchanged; let the CCB decide.
Ask the stakeholder to resubmit after the next milestone.
questions.explanation: RE should formally record the request and analyze impacts, but leave the approved baseline unchanged until the CCB decides. Rejecting the change exceeds RE authority; editing the baseline without approval violates its integrity.

questions.prompt: A use-case description for ‘Make a bank transfer’ includes an actor, a six-step main flow, and a postcondition (amount transferred). What REQUIRED element is missing?
options: A sequence diagram as a graphical supplement.
The precondition—the system state that must hold BEFORE the use case starts.
A complete list of all actors in the overall system.
A reference to the system architecture.
questions.explanation: The precondition states when the use case may start, for example that the user is logged in and has an active account with sufficient funds. Other common elements include name, actor, main and alternative flows, and postcondition.

questions.prompt: What is an ALTERNATIVE FLOW in a use-case description?
options: A second, parallel use case with a similar main flow.
An <<extend>> path in the use-case diagram showing optional extensions.
A path triggered when a main-flow step does not proceed as expected, such as invalid input, an error, or an exceptional case.
A use-case variant that applies only to certain actors.
questions.explanation: Alternative flows describe deviations from the main flow, including errors, exceptions, and boundary cases. For example, if a card is declined, document the system response and possible next actor actions.

questions.prompt: A stakeholder views a use-case diagram with eight use cases, four actors, and <<include>> relationships. What CANNOT be derived from the diagram?
options: Which actors initiate which use cases.
The system boundary and which functions it contains.
The concrete steps performed when the Customer starts ‘Place Order.’
Which use cases include other use cases.
questions.explanation: A use-case diagram is an overview showing actors, use-case names, relationships, and the system boundary. It does not show interaction steps, conditions, preconditions, postconditions, or alternative flows; these belong in the textual description.

questions.prompt: The development team asks: ‘What happens step by step when a user forgets their password, including all error cases?’ Which artifact answers this DIRECTLY?
options: The use-case diagram, which shows all system functions including ‘Reset password.’
The textual use-case description with its main flow and alternative flows, such as expired token or unknown email address.
A class diagram of user management.
The stakeholder list with roles and responsibilities.
questions.explanation: Only the textual use-case description contains the step-by-step main flow and alternative flows. A use-case diagram shows that the use case exists and which actor initiates it, but not flow details.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between a PRECONDITION and POSTCONDITION in a use-case description?
options: Precondition is the triggering event; postcondition is the final main-flow step.
Precondition is the system state required BEFORE the use case; postcondition is the state after SUCCESSFUL completion.
Both are optional metadata with no implementation impact.
Precondition names the primary actor; postcondition names the system feedback.
questions.explanation: A precondition describes what must be true before the use case starts, such as the user being logged in. A postcondition describes what must be true after successful completion, such as the order being stored. They support test preparation and success criteria.

questions.prompt: Why are BOTH a use-case diagram and a textual use-case description necessary instead of using only one form?
options: The diagram is for developers; the description is for testers.

The diagram gives the structural overview (actors, boundary, relationships); the description gives flow details (main and alternative flows, preconditions, and postconditions). They complement each other.
The description is mandatory; the diagram is optional and only useful for presentations.
They contain identical information in different forms, so either may be chosen by preference.
questions.explanation: The diagram shows which functions exist, who uses them, and how use cases relate. The description explains how a specific interaction proceeds, its conditions, and error paths. Both overview and detailed flow definition are needed for complete documentation and testability.

questions.prompt: A business department without UML knowledge must validate pricing logic with four input parameters and three discount levels. Which documentation model best suits this audience and purpose?
options: UML class diagram—shows the pricing data structures.
UML activity diagram—models the calculation flow with gateways.
Decision table—shows every condition combination and result in tabular form and can be validated without UML knowledge.
UML sequence diagram—shows component interactions during calculation.
questions.explanation: Choose a model according to both audience and purpose. A decision table suits conditional calculation logic and can be checked by business experts without UML training. Each row makes a condition combination and result explicit.

questions.prompt: A stakeholder wants to understand what data the system manages and how it relates, but NOT how processes run. Which model type fits?
options: Activity diagram—shows flows and decision points.
Sequence diagram—shows interactions between components over time.
Class diagram or entity-relationship diagram—structural models for data and relationships, without process or time dimensions.
State diagram—models states and transition conditions.
questions.explanation: Class diagrams and ERDs are structural models: they show entities, attributes, and relationships without a time dimension. Activity, sequence, and state diagrams model behavior.

questions.prompt: Which FOUR ROLES are defined in a formal inspection according to IREB?
options: Project manager, developer, tester, client.
Moderator, author, reviewer, and scribe—with a manager as an optional additional role.
Requirements engineer, reviewer, stakeholder, facilitator.
Inspector, observer, approver, coordinator.
questions.explanation: The four core roles are Moderator, Author, Reviewer, and Scribe. A Manager may be added to decide on resources and follow-up approval. Clear role separation is central to a Fagan inspection.

questions.prompt: What is the MAIN TASK of the SCRIBE in a formal inspection?
options: Review the document’s content and explain every defect.
Lead the meeting, structure discussion, and check entry criteria.
Record all findings raised during the inspection meeting completely and accurately.
Formally release the revised document after follow-up.
questions.explanation: The Scribe records findings raised in the meeting, including their locations and classifications. The Scribe does not act as a reviewer; the Moderator leads the meeting.

questions.prompt: Why must the document’s AUTHOR NOT also serve as MODERATOR?
options: The author knows the document too well to discover any new defects.
It creates a conflict of interest: the author may defend the document, while the moderator must lead neutrally and record findings objectively.
The author is responsible for corrections and has no time to moderate.
IREB requires the moderator to be from another department.
questions.explanation: Role separation is a quality feature of formal inspection. A neutral moderator encourages reviewers to raise criticism freely. If the author moderates, they may unintentionally steer discussion or downplay findings. Fagan inspection separates these roles.

questions.prompt: What is a REVIEWER required to do BEFORE an inspection meeting?
options: Read the document for the first time during the meeting and share spontaneous impressions.
Create a list of all stakeholders affected by the document.
Study the document individually, identify findings, and record them in preparation for the meeting.
Inform the moderator of all planned findings in advance so the agenda can be prepared.
questions.explanation: Individual preparation is a required phase and entry criterion for a formal inspection. Reviewers should analyze the document beforehand; unprepared attendance lowers defect detection and may require postponing the inspection.

questions.prompt: During an inspection, a reviewer reports that REQ-55 says ‘The system should respond quickly.’ How should this finding be classified?
options: No finding—‘quickly’ is an industry-standard term everyone understands.
Minor defect—the wording is weak, but the goal is clear and the document can be baselined.
Major defect—‘quickly’ is not measurable, so the requirement cannot be reliably tested or implemented; the document is not suitable as a baseline in this state.
Observation—an optional improvement with no process consequence.
questions.explanation: A major defect makes the document unsuitable as an implementation baseline. ‘Quickly’ is not measurable or unambiguous: developers cannot implement a precise target and testers cannot derive an objective test. It must be revised before baseline approval.

questions.prompt: After follow-up, the moderator confirms that the three original major defects were fixed correctly, but two new major problems arose during revision. What is the next action?
options: Release the document because all original findings were addressed.
Wait for the author to revise it again without further review.
Schedule a reinspection because new major defects require another formal review.
Record the new findings in follow-up and address them during implementation.
questions.explanation: Follow-up verifies corrections; it is not a full reinspection. New major defects mean the document is still unsuitable as a baseline, so a reinspection is required after revision.

questions.prompt: How does an ACCEPTANCE-TEST WORKSHOP as a validation technique differ from a traditional review?
options: The workshop checks source code; a review checks requirements documents.
Stakeholders jointly define and validate acceptance criteria—the goal is agreement on what ‘done’ means, not finding document defects.
Workshops happen after implementation; reviews always happen before it.
The author is absent from workshops but present in reviews.
questions.explanation: A review seeks defects in an artifact. An acceptance-test workshop establishes stakeholder agreement on concrete, measurable conditions for completion before implementation. Its outcome is shared understanding of success criteria, not a defect list.

questions.prompt: For which type of requirement are FORMAL METHODS most suitable as a validation technique?
options: User stories in agile projects, to help write acceptance criteria.
Stakeholder interviews, to structure meeting notes.
Safety-critical or mathematically precise requirements whose correctness must be formally proven, such as control software, medical devices, or cryptography.
All requirement types, because formal methods always provide the highest assurance.
questions.explanation: Formal methods support mathematical reasoning about specifications and are appropriate when failures could be catastrophic or mathematical precision is essential. For ordinary business requirements, their cost often outweighs the benefit.

questions.prompt: The Kano model distinguishes three main categories. Which names are CORRECT?
options: Must-have, Should-have, Could-have.
Basic attributes, performance attributes, and excitement attributes.
Core features, extension features, and innovation features.
Functional requirements, quality requirements, and constraints.
questions.explanation: Kano categories are basic attributes, whose absence causes dissatisfaction; performance attributes, where better performance increases satisfaction; and excitement attributes, which delight when present but are not expected. Kano classifies satisfaction potential, not implementation order.

questions.prompt: Online-shop users never praise ‘View my orders’ because they take it for granted, but complain strongly if it is missing. Which Kano category applies?
options: Excitement attribute—users are delighted when it is implemented especially well.
Performance attribute—better implementation creates more satisfaction.
Basic attribute—users expect it; its presence goes unnoticed, while its absence causes strong dissatisfaction.
Indifferent attribute—users show little reaction either way.
questions.explanation: A basic attribute has an asymmetric effect: when present it is taken for granted; when absent it causes dissatisfaction. Such requirements may not be mentioned in interviews, so RE should actively identify them.

questions.prompt: A navigation app offers AI-generated stories about sights along the current route. Users who discover them are delighted; users who do not know about them do not miss them. Which Kano category applies?
options: Basic attribute—every navigation app needs content beyond navigation.
Performance attribute—more stories mean more satisfaction.
Excitement attribute—unexpected and delightful when present; its absence causes no dissatisfaction.
Dissatisfier—the feature reduces satisfaction when absent.
questions.explanation: An excitement attribute is unexpected and delights users when present, while its absence causes no dissatisfaction. Over time, excitement attributes may become performance and eventually basic attributes as expectations change.

questions.prompt: REQ-004: ‘The system MUST implement GDPR-compliant deletion of data after 3 years; a violation could incur a fine of up to 4% of annual revenue.’ Which MoSCoW category applies?
options: Should Have—important, but deliverable in a later release.
Could Have—useful but dispensable if time is short.
Must Have—non-negotiable legal compliance whose absence blocks success or operation.
Won’t Have—not in scope now, but planned for a future release.
questions.explanation: A Must Have is one without which the system cannot be delivered or the consequences of omission are unacceptable. Legal GDPR compliance is mandatory, not optional or deferrable.

questions.prompt: A Product Owner asks: ‘Which requirements should I NOT put into the next sprint because they are likely to change?’ Which attribute gives the MOST DIRECT answer?
options: Priority—indicates which requirements should be implemented first.
Status—indicates the process stage of a requirement.
Stability—indicates how likely a requirement is to change.
Version—indicates how many times a requirement has changed.
questions.explanation: The stability attribute directly indicates expected change likelihood. Low or unstable requirements increase the risk of rework if planned into a sprint. Version history is only an indirect indicator of future stability.

questions.prompt: A QA manager asks: ‘Show me all requirements that are implemented but do not yet have a test case.’ Which attribute directly filters this set?
options: Priority—shows implementation order.
Version—shows the current requirement version.
Status—filters requirements marked ‘implemented’ from the full set.
Source—shows which stakeholder introduced the requirement.
questions.explanation: Status is a lifecycle attribute with states such as proposed, approved, implemented, tested, and accepted. Filtering by ‘implemented’ identifies the requirements requested. Status supports progress and gap tracking.

questions.prompt: Consider the context diagram. What does the arrow from ‘Tax office’ to ‘Accounting system’ represent?
options: The tax office has read access to all accounting data.
The system sends accounting data to the tax office.
The accounting system receives data from the tax office, such as tax rules or reporting requirements.
The tax office is the system’s client.
questions.explanation: In a context diagram, an incoming arrow indicates a flow into the system. Here the accounting system receives information such as tax rates or reporting formats from the tax office. An outgoing arrow would show system output to an external entity.

questions.prompt: This use-case diagram contains a modeling error. What is WRONG?
options: Use case ‘Check payment’ is missing an <<include>> relationship.
The ‘Back office’ actor is inside the system boundary; actors must be outside the system boundary.
The ‘Customer’ actor must also be drawn inside the system boundary.
The diagram has too few use cases for a real system.
questions.explanation: Actors represent external roles that interact with the system and therefore belong outside the system boundary. Placing an actor inside the boundary is a fundamental modeling error.

questions.prompt: The state diagram shows an order lifecycle. From which state is a direct transition to ‘Cancelled’ NOT possible according to the diagram?
options: Open.
Completed.
Paid.
None—all states can be cancelled directly.
questions.explanation: According to the described diagram, an Open order can transition to Cancelled, but no cancellation transition is shown from Paid. Completed is also terminal, but the stated answer identifies the missing cancellation path from Paid.

questions.prompt: Which BPMN gateway type is shown in the diagram, and what does it mean?
options: Parallel gateway (AND)—all three payment routes run simultaneously.
Inclusive gateway (OR)—at least one payment route is selected.
Exclusive gateway (XOR)—exactly one payment route is selected; the X marks this type.
Event-based gateway—the first payment event determines the route.
questions.explanation: An X in the gateway symbol indicates an exclusive (XOR) gateway, where exactly one outgoing path is selected. An AND gateway uses a plus sign; an OR gateway uses a circle.

questions.prompt: The diagram shows two use-case relationships. Which statement is correct?
options: Both arrows point in the same direction, which is correct for include and extend.
Relationship A is wrong: for <<include>>, the arrow must originate at the included use case.
Both arrows are correct: <<include>> points from the base use case to the included use case; <<extend>> points from the extension use case to the base use case.
Relationship B is wrong: <<extend>> arrows must originate at the base use case.
questions.explanation: For <<include>>, the arrow goes from the base use case to the obligatorily included use case. For <<extend>>, it goes from the optional extension use case to the base use case. The opposite directions are intentional.

questions.prompt: What does the INVEST criterion for user stories stand for?
options: An estimation method for story points.
Qualities of good user stories: Independent, Negotiable, Valuable, Estimable, Small, Testable.
A framework for prioritizing the Product Backlog by business value.
The six mandatory parts of a formal requirements specification.
questions.explanation: INVEST means Independent, Negotiable, Valuable, Estimable, Small, and Testable. A good user story should satisfy all six criteria.

questions.prompt: A team uses DOORS to version, link, and prioritize requirements, but 40% are ambiguous and untestable. What explains this problem?
options: DOORS is no longer suitable for agile projects.
The team should have used a modeling tool.
RM tools manage requirements but do not automatically improve their content quality.
The traceability links were configured incorrectly.
questions.explanation: RM tools store, link, and version requirements. Poor requirements remain poor; the tool does not automatically detect or correct content defects. Quality depends on RE competence, process, and reviews.

questions.prompt: ‘The system shall respond in under 2 seconds with 1,000 concurrent users.’ What type of requirement is this?
options: Functional requirement—it describes WHAT the system does.
Quality (non-functional) requirement—it describes a measurable performance property.
Constraint—an external restriction on the system.
Design requirement—it specifies the technical implementation.
questions.explanation: Response time is a performance quality attribute, so this is a quality requirement. Functional requirements describe system functions. Measurability does not make a requirement functional.

questions.prompt: ‘The system SOLL provide an export function.’ What does ‘SOLL’ mean in normative IREB German?
options: Recommended but optional.
Mandatory—the requirement must be fulfilled.
Required only if budget is available.
Equivalent to ‘may’—permitted but not required.
questions.explanation: In normative German usage, ‘soll’ corresponds to ‘shall’ and is mandatory. ‘Sollte’ means recommended; ‘darf’ corresponds to optional ‘may’. Confusing ‘soll’ and ‘sollte’ changes the requirement’s binding force.

questions.prompt: ‘As an accountant, I want to export monthly reports as PDFs.’ Is this a stakeholder requirement or a system requirement?
options: System requirement—it describes a specific system function.
Stakeholder requirement—it expresses a need without specifying the technical implementation.
Constraint—an external restriction.
Quality requirement—a system performance property.
questions.explanation: Stakeholder requirements express what a person needs without prescribing technical details. System requirements are derived from these needs and specify how the system will satisfy them.

questions.prompt: Which is a QUALITY (non-functional) requirement?
options: The system shall authenticate users.
The system shall provide a search function.
The system shall be available 99.9% of the time.
The system shall store orders.
questions.explanation: Availability of 99.9% is a quality attribute. Authentication, search, and order storage describe functions. Quality requirements specify HOW WELL; functional requirements specify WHAT.

questions.prompt: What distinguishes a CONSTRAINT from a QUALITY REQUIREMENT?
options: Constraints are always more expensive to implement.
A constraint restricts the solution space (for example, through a technology mandate or law) without describing system quality.
Quality requirements are measurable, while constraints are not.
Constraints are stated only by external stakeholders.
questions.explanation: A constraint restricts the solution space, such as requiring Java, rather than describing how well the system performs. A quality requirement describes a quality attribute such as response time or availability. Both can be measurable and may come from external parties.

questions.prompt: Which TWO statements correctly describe a STAKEHOLDER in the IREB sense?
options: Stakeholders are only direct end users who work with the system daily.
Stakeholders may have direct or indirect interests in the system’s requirements.
Regulatory authorities are typical stakeholders even if they never use the system.
Stakeholders are only people with a contractual relationship with the client.
questions.explanation: Stakeholders include parties with direct or indirect influence on requirements or affected by the system. Regulatory authorities are indirect stakeholders because they can impose binding requirements without using the system. Restricting the definition to end users or contract partners is too narrow.

questions.prompt: Which TWO statements about QUALITY REQUIREMENTS (non-functional requirements) are correct in the IREB reference model?
options: Quality requirements are always optional and need be implemented only if time and budget permit.
Quality requirements describe how well the system should perform a function.
Quality requirements may include performance, reliability, and security aspects.
Quality requirements describe only the system’s user interface.
questions.explanation: Quality requirements describe how well a function is performed and cover attributes such as performance, reliability, security, availability, and maintainability. They are not necessarily optional and are not limited to the user interface.

questions.prompt: Which TWO techniques are ESPECIALLY suitable for uncovering tacit knowledge?
options: A written multiple-choice questionnaire.
Field observation of stakeholders in their real work environment.
Prototyping followed by feedback sessions.
Analysis of existing process manuals.
questions.explanation: Field observation reveals actual workflows stakeholders may not be able to describe. Prototyping externalizes implicit expectations through reactions to a concrete model. Questionnaires rely on verbalizable knowledge; document analysis mainly reveals explicit, codified knowledge.

questions.prompt: Which TWO statements about the SYSTEM BOUNDARY are correct?
options: The system boundary defines which parts of reality belong to the system and which belong to its environment (context).
The chosen software architecture technically determines the system boundary.
