Everything inside the system boundary is within the project scope and is designed and implemented by the team.
Only the client sets the system boundary, and it cannot change during the project.
questions.explanation: The system boundary separates the system from its context and defines project scope. It is a negotiated scope decision, not a technical consequence of architecture, and may change through project negotiation.

questions.prompt: A requirement says: ‘The system should respond performantly when needed and comply with all security standards.’ Which TWO quality criteria are violated?
options: Consistency—‘performant’ and ‘secure’ are inherently contradictory.
Atomicity—multiple quality attributes (performance and security) are combined in one requirement.
Testability—‘when needed’ and ‘performantly’ are subjective and not objectively measurable.
Completeness—implementation details are missing.
questions.explanation: Atomicity is violated because performance and security are separate attributes that should be prioritized and tested separately. Testability is also violated because the requirement gives no measurable condition or threshold. The other options do not describe the primary problems.

questions.prompt: Which TWO statements about a formal INSPECTION (such as a Fagan inspection) are correct?
options: A formal inspection follows a structured process with defined roles such as moderator, author, reviewer, and scribe.
The author also moderates the inspection to save time.
Formal inspections use checklists and collect defect metrics.
Formal inspections do not require individual reviewer preparation.
questions.explanation: Formal inspections define separate roles, use checklists and defect metrics, and require individual reviewer preparation. The author and moderator are distinct roles.

questions.prompt: Which TWO activities explicitly belong to REQUIREMENTS MANAGEMENT?
options: Versioning requirements and maintaining change history.
Initially eliciting requirements through stakeholder interviews.
Creating UML models of system structure.
Maintaining traceability throughout the project.
questions.explanation: Requirements management includes versioning, change history, status tracking, traceability, and change management. Initial elicitation is a separate RE activity; UML modeling belongs to documentation.

questions.prompt: Which TWO modeling notations are suitable for describing a system’s DYNAMIC BEHAVIOR?
options: Entity-relationship diagram (ERD).
State machine diagram.
UML class diagram.
Sequence diagram.
questions.explanation: State machines describe changes between states over time; sequence diagrams describe the temporal order of messages between components. ERDs and class diagrams model static structure.

questions.prompt: Which TWO statements about REQUIREMENTS PRIORITIZATION are correct?
options: Prioritization assigns each requirement to a developer.
Prioritization helps implement the most important requirements first when resources are limited.
Prioritization can be used to manage scope when constraints arise.
Prioritization replaces requirements validation.
questions.explanation: Prioritization expresses relative value or urgency and supports resource allocation and scope management. It does not assign developers or replace validation.

questions.prompt: Which TWO statements about REQUIREMENTS WORKSHOPS as an elicitation technique are correct?
options: Workshops let stakeholders discuss conflicts directly and work toward agreement.
Workshops need neither moderation nor preparation.
Workshops are suitable only for eliciting technical requirements.
Workshops promote shared understanding of the problem among stakeholders.
questions.explanation: Workshops bring stakeholders together to discuss conflicts and build a shared problem understanding. They need preparation and moderation, and can elicit functional as well as quality requirements.

questions.prompt: Which TWO statements about documenting requirements in NATURAL LANGUAGE are correct?
options: Natural language is accessible to stakeholders regardless of technical background.
Natural-language requirements are always more precise than formal models.
Natural language is suitable only for non-functional requirements.
Natural-language requirements are prone to ambiguity and differing interpretations.
questions.explanation: Natural language is accessible without specialized notation knowledge, but inherently prone to ambiguity. Formal notations can be more precise; natural language can describe both functional and quality requirements.

questions.prompt: Which TWO statements about FIELD OBSERVATION (ethnographic elicitation) are correct?
options: It is useful when stakeholders cannot fully describe how they work.
It produces only quantitative, statistically analyzable data.
It can reveal tacit knowledge that interviews may not uncover.
It completely replaces all other elicitation techniques in every project.
questions.explanation: Field observation reveals tacit knowledge and actual practices that stakeholders may not be able to articulate. It mainly produces qualitative data and complements rather than replaces other techniques.

questions.prompt: Which TWO consequences typically arise when requirements are NOT TESTABLE?
options: The Change Control Board automatically stops the project.
It is impossible to determine objectively whether the requirement has been met.
Stakeholders automatically reject untestable requirements.
Meaningful test cases cannot be derived for the requirement.
questions.explanation: Untestable requirements prevent objective assessment of fulfillment and meaningful test-case derivation. They do not automatically stop a project or cause automatic stakeholder rejection.

questions.prompt: Which TWO factors typically belong to the SYSTEM CONTEXT?
options: External systems that exchange data with the system being developed.
The system’s internal database schema.
Legal and regulatory requirements the system must meet.
The system’s internal software architecture.
questions.explanation: External systems and legal regulations are outside influences and belong to the context. The internal database schema and software architecture are inside the system boundary.

questions.prompt: Which TWO activities are CORE ELEMENTS of formal CHANGE MANAGEMENT?
options: Eliciting new requirements in stakeholder workshops.
Creating UML diagrams for every changed requirement.
Analyzing the change’s impact on existing requirements and downstream artifacts.
Obtaining formal approval from an authorized body, such as a Change Control Board.
questions.explanation: Formal change management includes impact analysis and approval by an authorized decision-maker. Elicitation is a separate RE activity; UML diagrams may document changes but are not mandatory change-management steps.

questions.prompt: Which TWO statements about the REQUIREMENTS ENGINEERING PROCESS are correct?
options: RE is iterative—activities repeat and influence one another.
RE formally ends when the system-analysis phase is complete.
RE activities can occur in parallel and overlap.
RE is exclusively the responsibility of the requirements engineer.
questions.explanation: RE is iterative and its activities may overlap. It continues throughout the project and involves stakeholders, Product Owners, developers, testers, and other roles—not only the requirements engineer.

questions.prompt: Which TWO statements about USE CASES are correct?
options: Use cases model only a system’s internal data structures.
Use cases describe system behavior from the actors’ perspective and their interactions with the system.
A use case can describe a main flow as well as alternative and exception scenarios.
Use cases are suitable only for traditional waterfall projects.
questions.explanation: Use cases describe external system behavior from an actor’s perspective and may include main, alternative, and exception flows. They do not model internal data structures and are method-agnostic.

questions.prompt: Which TWO statements about REQUIREMENTS CONSISTENCY are correct?
options: Consistency requires that no requirement contradicts another in the specification.
Consistency matters only when requirements come from different stakeholders.
Contradictions arise only from unclear wording, never from conflicting stakeholder interests.
Traceability matrices and systematic reviews can help check consistency.
questions.explanation: Consistency means requirements do not contradict one another. Traceability matrices and reviews can help reveal inconsistencies. Consistency matters regardless of source, and conflicts often result from genuinely differing stakeholder interests.

questions.prompt: Which TWO techniques are used for REQUIREMENTS VALIDATION?
options: Brainstorming sessions to generate ideas for new features.
Reviews (inspection, walkthrough, technical review).
Prototyping to obtain early stakeholder feedback.
Entity-relationship diagrams for data modeling.
questions.explanation: Reviews systematically check requirements, while prototypes let stakeholders assess whether a concrete model reflects their needs. Brainstorming is elicitation; ER modeling documents structure rather than validating requirements.

questions.prompt: Which TWO challenges are TYPICAL of STAKEHOLDER ANALYSIS?
options: Stakeholder groups may be overlooked, leading to missing or incorrect requirements.
All stakeholders always have complete and consistent requirements ready.
Different stakeholder groups may have conflicting or contradictory requirements.
Stakeholder analysis matters only in projects with more than 100 stakeholders.
questions.explanation: Overlooked stakeholders create blind spots, and competing interests often cause conflicting requirements that need negotiation. Stakeholder analysis is relevant in every project; stakeholders rarely have complete and consistent needs ready.

questions.prompt: Which TWO statements about documenting QUALITY REQUIREMENTS are correct?
options: Quality requirements must be implemented as separate system components.
Quality requirements should contain measurable criteria so fulfillment can be demonstrated.
Quality requirements can be documented only in formal notations, not natural language.
Quality requirements can constrain or influence how functional requirements are implemented.
questions.explanation: Measurable quality requirements are testable, and attributes such as security or performance can influence implementation of functions. They need not be separate components, and natural language is permitted.

questions.prompt: Which TWO statements about CREATIVITY TECHNIQUES in requirements elicitation are correct?
options: Techniques such as brainstorming are especially useful early, while the solution space is still open.
They can reveal innovative requirements that traditional interviews may not uncover.
They fundamentally replace every other elicitation technique.
They always produce complete requirements ready for implementation.
questions.explanation: Creativity techniques support idea generation, particularly early in a project, and can reveal ideas interviews miss. They complement other techniques and produce material that still needs refinement.

questions.prompt: Which TWO statements about REQUIREMENTS TRACEABILITY are correct?
options: Traceability is relevant only to safety-critical systems such as medical or aviation systems.
Traceability supports impact analysis when requirements change.
Traceability is established only backward to requirement sources.
Traceability can be established forward to design, code, and tests and backward to sources and stakeholders.
questions.explanation: Traceability identifies artifacts affected by changes and can be established in both directions. It is useful across project types, not only in safety-critical domains.

questions.prompt: Which TWO statements about the RE core activity DOCUMENTATION are correct?
options: Requirements documentation can include natural-language and model-based representations.
Requirements documentation replaces ongoing communication with stakeholders.
Requirements documentation must always contain UML diagrams.
Its goal is to record requirements clearly and unambiguously for relevant stakeholders.
questions.explanation: Documentation can use text and models and aims to record requirements understandably and unambiguously. It supports rather than replaces communication; UML is an option, not mandatory.

questions.prompt: Which TWO statements about RESOLVING CONFLICTING REQUIREMENTS are correct?
options: The project manager should always decide alone without involving stakeholders.
Structured negotiation among the affected stakeholders is a legitimate resolution strategy.
If consensus cannot be reached, escalate the conflict to an authorized decision-maker.
Conflicts arise only from language misunderstandings, never from genuine competing interests.
questions.explanation: Negotiation with affected stakeholders is preferred; if it fails, escalation is appropriate. Unilateral decisions and assuming all conflicts are merely linguistic are incorrect.

questions.prompt: Which TWO notations describe a system’s STRUCTURE?
options: UML class diagram.
Sequence diagram.
Entity-relationship diagram (ERD).
UML activity diagram.
questions.explanation: Class diagrams and ERDs model static structure, including entities, attributes, and relationships. Sequence and activity diagrams describe behavior.

questions.prompt: Which TWO characteristics describe a well-written natural-language requirement?
options: It contains detailed technical implementation descriptions.
It is unambiguous and permits only one interpretation.
It combines as many conditions as possible to reduce documentation effort.
It is testable so fulfillment can be demonstrated objectively.
questions.explanation: Unambiguity and testability are important quality criteria. Implementation details belong in design documents, and combining conditions violates atomicity.

questions.prompt: Which TWO statements about PROTOTYPING as an elicitation technique are correct?
options: Prototyping helps externalize stakeholders’ tacit knowledge.
Prototyping is useful only after a complete requirements specification exists.
Prototyping is especially valuable when stakeholders cannot verbalize their requirements.
Prototypes must always be fully coded, runnable software systems.
questions.explanation: Prototyping helps reveal implicit expectations through reactions to a model, especially when stakeholders struggle to articulate requirements. It can be used before a complete specification, and paper prototypes or mockups are often sufficient.

questions.prompt: Which TWO of the following are IREB CORE ACTIVITIES of the RE process?
options: System design and architecture decisions.
Requirements elicitation.
Deployment and commissioning.
Requirements validation and review.
questions.explanation: IREB’s four core activities are elicitation, documentation, validation/review, and management. System design belongs to systems engineering; deployment and commissioning belong to delivery and operations.

questions.prompt: Which TWO statements correctly distinguish a USE-CASE DIAGRAM from a USE-CASE SCENARIO?
options: A use-case diagram shows every detailed interaction step between actor and system.
A use-case diagram gives an overview of actors, system boundary, use-case names, and relationships.
A use-case scenario describes the concrete steps of one particular flow, main or alternative.
Use-case scenarios are used only for error cases.
questions.explanation: The diagram is an overview, not a step-by-step description. A scenario describes a specific interaction flow and may cover normal or alternative cases.

questions.prompt: Which TWO statements about USER STORIES in agile RE are correct?
options: A user story is a formal UML diagram describing system functions.
A user story briefly describes a system function from a user’s perspective: ‘As [role], I want [goal], so that [benefit].’
Acceptance criteria make user stories testable and define when a story is done.
User stories replace all other RE documentation in agile projects.
questions.explanation: User stories use the role/goal/benefit format and describe functionality from a user perspective. Acceptance criteria define fulfillment conditions and support testing. Stories are not UML diagrams and do not replace all other documentation.

questions.prompt: Which TWO statements about a BASELINE in requirements management are correct?
options: A baseline permanently freezes all requirements; changes are no longer possible.
A baseline is an agreed and reviewed requirements state that serves as a reference for project activities.
Changes after a baseline is agreed must be controlled through a formal change process.
A baseline is created only at the end of the project.
questions.explanation: A baseline is an approved reference state. Changes remain possible but must follow a formal change process. Baselines can be established at different milestones, not only at project end.

questions.prompt: A team discusses (a) ‘The system must authenticate users using OAuth 2.0’ and (b) ‘The system must respond to search queries within 1 second.’ Which TWO classification statements are correct?
options: (a) is functional and (b) is a quality requirement—this is one reasonable classification.
(a) can be classified as a constraint because OAuth 2.0 restricts the solution space.
(b) is functional because it describes what the system should do.
Both are functional because they use the word ‘must.’
questions.explanation: (a) describes authentication and may also be viewed as a constraint because it mandates OAuth 2.0. (b) is a performance quality requirement. The modal verb alone does not determine requirement type.

questions.prompt: Which TWO statements correctly distinguish VALIDATION from VERIFICATION?
options: Validation checks whether implementation conforms to documented requirements.
Validation checks whether documented requirements reflect actual stakeholder needs.
Verification asks ‘Are we building the system right?’ (implementation conforms to specification).
Validation and verification are synonyms in IREB terminology.
questions.explanation: Validation asks whether requirements reflect stakeholder needs; verification checks whether implementation conforms to requirements. The terms describe distinct activities.

questions.prompt: A team must model (1) order states (open, processing, completed, cancelled) and (2) the message sequence between customer and ordering system. Which TWO notations are suitable?
options: Class diagram for (1) and activity diagram for (2).
State machine for (1) and sequence diagram for (2).
Use-case diagram for (1) and context diagram for (2).
Sequence diagram for (1) and state machine for (2).
questions.explanation: A state machine models an object’s states; a sequence diagram models message order between actors and systems. Note: the source key lists the same option index twice; it is represented here once as the single correct combination.

questions.prompt: Which TWO statements about requirements documentation in AGILE PROJECTS are correct?
options: Agile projects document requirements only in a complete specification prepared in advance.
User stories, acceptance criteria, and backlog items are typical agile RE documentation forms.
Requirements are refined and adapted iteratively in agile projects.
Agile methods reject all requirements documentation.
questions.explanation: Agile RE commonly documents requirements as user stories, acceptance criteria, and backlog items, refining them iteratively and just in time. Agile methods do not reject documentation, but adapt it.

questions.prompt: In which TWO scenarios is PROTOTYPING especially suitable as an elicitation technique?
options: A detailed requirements specification is already complete.
Stakeholders struggle to verbalize their requirements.
A novel product is being developed without reference systems.
Only quantitative data for prioritization is needed.
questions.explanation: Prototyping helps externalize tacit knowledge and makes vague ideas concrete, particularly for novel products. It is not primarily intended for collecting only quantitative prioritization data or when a complete specification already exists.

questions.prompt: Which TWO statements correctly describe the SYSTEM CONTEXT?
options: The system context is the relevant part of the environment outside the system boundary.
The system context includes internal modules and subsystems of the system being developed.
Context elements are not under the development team’s direct control.
The system context is identical to the system architecture.
questions.explanation: The system context consists of relevant external elements. These are outside the development team’s direct control and must be treated as given conditions. Internal modules and architecture belong to the system itself.

questions.prompt: Which TWO statements about the KANO MODEL as a prioritization technique are correct?
options: The Kano model classifies requirements by their contribution to customer satisfaction.
The Kano model uses Must/Should/Could/Won’t categories.
Excitement attributes (delighters) describe requirements that pleasantly surprise customers.
The Kano model is suitable only for hardware products.
questions.explanation: Kano evaluates how requirements affect customer satisfaction. Excitement attributes pleasantly surprise users. Must/Should/Could/Won’t is MoSCoW, and Kano applies to software and hardware.

questions.prompt: Which TWO roles are characteristic of a formal INSPECTION?
options: The author, who created the document and explains it during the review.
The moderator, who leads the inspection independently of the author.
The client, who approves every defect found.
The reviewer/inspector, who prepares individually and examines the document.
questions.explanation: The moderator and reviewers are core inspection roles; reviewers prepare individually. The author may attend but does not moderate, and the client is not a required inspection role.

questions.prompt: Which TWO of the following requirements are CONSTRAINTS?
options: The system must process transactions in under 500 ms.
The system must be implemented in Python 3.11.
The system must use encrypted connections for all database access.
The system may use only open-source libraries under the Apache 2.0 license.
questions.explanation: Mandating Python 3.11 restricts implementation technology, and limiting libraries by license restricts tool choice; both are constraints. Transaction time is a performance quality requirement, while encrypted connections express a security quality requirement.

questions.prompt: Which TWO statements about UML USE-CASE RELATIONSHIPS are correct?
options: <<include>> models an optional extension under specified conditions.
<<include>> expresses mandatory inclusion: the base use case is incomplete without the included use case.
<<extend>> models a conditional, optional extension of a base use case.
<<extend>> and <<include>> are interchangeable and have the same meaning.
questions.explanation: <<include>> is mandatory; the included use case is always executed. <<extend>> is optional and conditional. They have different meanings and are not interchangeable.

questions.prompt: Which TWO statements about REQUIREMENTS NEGOTIATION are correct?
options: It aims for a consensus or compromise acceptable to all parties.
The most influential stakeholder always prevails.
It can be supported by structured dialogue, facilitation, or escalation.
It is relevant only in traditional waterfall projects.
questions.explanation: Negotiation seeks an agreed compromise and may use facilitation or escalation to an authorized decision-maker. Unilateral dominance is not a professional negotiation outcome, and negotiation applies across development approaches.

questions.prompt: Which TWO statements about SHALL/SHOULD/MAY wording in requirements specifications are correct?
options: ‘Shall’ marks mandatory requirements that must be fulfilled.
‘Should’ is just as binding as ‘shall.’
Using these modal verbs consistently clearly distinguishes obligation from recommendation.
‘May’ marks a mandatory requirement with lower priority.
questions.explanation: ‘Shall’ is mandatory, ‘should’ is recommended but not required, and ‘may’ is optional. Consistent usage prevents confusion about binding force.

questions.prompt: Which TWO functions are TYPICAL of a REQUIREMENTS MANAGEMENT TOOL (RM tool)?
options: Automatic code generation from requirements.
Requirement versioning with change history.
Creating traceability links among requirements, test cases, and design artifacts.
Automatically testing whether the system satisfies every requirement.
questions.explanation: RM tools commonly provide versioning and traceability. Code generation belongs to model-driven engineering; automated system testing belongs to testing tools and processes.

questions.prompt: Which TWO consequences typically arise if CONTRADICTORY requirements are not resolved?
options: Developers must make arbitrary decisions about which requirement to follow.
The system is automatically built according to the higher-priority requirement.
Inconsistent system behavior may result because different components implement different requirements.
The client is automatically notified and decides the conflict.
questions.explanation: Unresolved contradictions shift decisions to developers and can cause inconsistent behavior across components. Neither automatic resolution nor automatic client notification occurs.

questions.prompt: A team is replacing a 20-year-old legacy system whose clerks know it by heart. Which TWO elicitation risks are especially high?
options: Stakeholders know their requirements too well, so no unknown requirements exist.
Stakeholders describe features of the old system (‘the way it has always worked’) instead of underlying needs.
Tacit knowledge about workarounds and special cases may not be verbalized.
There are too many stakeholders for elicitation to be completed.
questions.explanation: Stakeholders may be biased toward reproducing the legacy system and may fail to mention implicit workarounds or special rules. Context interviews, observation, and process analysis can help uncover underlying needs.

questions.prompt: Which TWO statements about different REVIEW TYPES are correct?
options: A walkthrough is more formal than an inspection and requires more preparation.
An informal review is the least formal review type and does not require defined roles.
A technical review is intermediate in formality between a walkthrough and a formal inspection.
All review types achieve the same defect-detection rate when experts participate.
questions.explanation: Informal reviews are the least structured; technical reviews are more formal than walkthroughs but less formal than inspections. Formal inspections generally achieve higher defect-detection rates due to their structure and preparation.

questions.prompt: What are TWO purposes of a STAKEHOLDER MAP (for example, an onion diagram)?
options: It shows which stakeholder has the highest decision authority in the project.
It visualizes stakeholders’ proximity to the system and helps identify all relevant stakeholders.
It serves as a communication aid to show stakeholders their influence on the project.
It replaces the requirements specification in early project phases.
questions.explanation: A stakeholder map visualizes stakeholders relative to the system and supports identification of overlooked groups. It is an analysis and communication aid, but does not automatically show decision authority or replace a specification.

questions.prompt: Which TWO of the following are typical REQUIREMENTS ARTIFACTS?
options: A development team’s sprint burndown chart.
A traceability matrix linking requirements to test cases.
A use-case diagram showing system boundaries and actors.
A deployment diagram of production infrastructure.
questions.explanation: A traceability matrix and a use-case diagram are RE artifacts. A burndown chart belongs to agile project management; a deployment diagram describes architecture or infrastructure.

questions.prompt: Which TWO activities are typical parts of STAKEHOLDER ANALYSIS?
options: Identify relevant stakeholder groups and their interests in the system.
Define the system’s technical architecture.
Assess each stakeholder group’s influence and impact.
Create the project work breakdown structure for development.
questions.explanation: Stakeholder analysis identifies relevant parties and their interests, then assesses their influence and impact, often using an influence-interest matrix. Architecture and work breakdown planning are separate activities.

questions.prompt: Which TWO elements are typically shown in a CONTEXT DIAGRAM (DFD Level 0)?
options: The system’s internal database structures.
The system being developed as a single black-box process.
External entities (actors or systems) exchanging data with the system.
Internal process steps of system functions.
questions.explanation: A context diagram shows the system as an undifferentiated black box and external entities with data flows across the boundary. Internal databases and process steps appear in more detailed DFD levels.

questions.prompt: Which TWO statements about roles in a formal INSPECTION are correct?
options: The author may also moderate to shorten the meeting.
The moderator leads the inspection process and ensures all phases are followed.
The scribe records defects and comments during the inspection meeting.
Reviewers create the document together with the author.
questions.explanation: The moderator leads the process and ensures phase discipline; the scribe records findings. The author and moderator must be different people, and reviewers inspect rather than create the document.

questions.prompt: Which TWO metrics are typically collected in formal INSPECTIONS to measure their effectiveness?
options: The number of requirements unchanged after inspection.
Defect density (defects per page or per requirement).
Preparation rate (preparation time per page or requirement for each reviewer).
The number of developers involved in implementation.
questions.explanation: Defect density indicates problem areas in a document; preparation rate indicates whether reviewers prepared sufficiently and serves as an efficiency measure. The other options are not inspection-effectiveness metrics.

questions.prompt: Which TWO statements correctly compare MoSCoW and the KANO MODEL as prioritization methods?
options: MoSCoW categorizes requirements by urgency as Must/Should/Could/Won’t and supports scope management.
Kano classifies basic, performance, and excitement attributes by their effect on customer satisfaction.
Both MoSCoW and Kano directly produce a numerical ranking of all requirements.
Kano completely replaces MoSCoW whenever user satisfaction is the focus.
questions.explanation: MoSCoW groups requirements by release urgency; Kano categorizes their effect on customer satisfaction. Both provide categories rather than a complete numerical ranking, and they are complementary methods.

questions.prompt: Which TWO are typical REQUIREMENT ATTRIBUTES describing a requirement’s lifecycle?
options: Requirement status, such as proposed, approved, implemented, or obsolete.
The name of the developer who implemented the requirement.
The requirement source, such as the stakeholder or document that introduced it.
The number of commit messages related to the requirement.
questions.explanation: Status tracks lifecycle state; source identifies where the requirement originated and supports traceability. Developer names and commit counts are implementation or version-control metadata, not typical RE attributes.

questions.prompt: Which TWO notations describe a system’s STATIC STRUCTURE rather than its dynamic behavior?
options: UML class diagram.
Sequence diagram.
Entity-relationship diagram (ERD).
Activity diagram.
questions.explanation: Class diagrams and ERDs model static structure, including entities, attributes, and relationships. Sequence and activity diagrams model dynamic behavior and flow.

questions.prompt: Which TWO quality criteria primarily apply to an INDIVIDUAL requirement rather than to the overall specification?
options: Completeness of the requirement—all information needed for implementation and testing is present.
Completeness of the specification—all necessary requirements are included in the document.
Testability—the requirement has a measurable threshold or verifiable acceptance criterion.
Specification consistency—requirements do not contradict one another.
questions.explanation: Completeness of an individual requirement and testability apply at requirement level. Specification completeness and consistency describe the document as a whole.

questions.prompt: Which TWO of the following are among IREB’s FOUR CORE RE ACTIVITIES?
options: Requirements elicitation.
System design and architecture planning.
Requirements documentation.
System deployment and operations.
questions.explanation: IREB’s four core activities are elicitation, documentation, validation/review, and management. System design belongs to systems engineering; deployment belongs to operations.

questions.prompt: Which TWO are quality criteria for an INDIVIDUAL requirement?
options: Atomicity—the requirement describes exactly one property.
Specification completeness—the document contains all necessary requirements.
Testability—the requirement can be tested objectively.
Traceability—the requirement is linked to test cases.
questions.explanation: Atomicity and testability are individual-requirement quality criteria. Specification completeness is a document-level property; traceability is a management concept, not an intrinsic quality criterion.

questions.prompt: Which TWO are defined roles in a formal inspection?
options: Moderator.
Product Owner.
Scribe.
Release Manager.
questions.explanation: Formal inspection roles include moderator, author, scribe, and reviewers. Product Owner and Release Manager are not defined inspection roles.

questions.prompt: Which TWO statements correctly describe TRACEABILITY?
options: Traceability links requirements to test cases and shows how requirements are tested.
Traceability automatically updates linked artifacts whenever a requirement changes.
Traceability supports impact analysis by identifying artifacts affected by a change.
Traceability guarantees that every requirement was correctly implemented.
questions.explanation: Traceability links requirements to related artifacts and supports change impact analysis. Automatic updates are tool-specific, and traceability alone does not guarantee correct implementation.

questions.prompt: Which TWO of the following are NOT RE ARTIFACTS?
options: A glossary defining project terminology.
A development team’s sprint burndown chart.
A stakeholder map.
A continuous-integration pipeline script.
questions.explanation: Burndown charts belong to agile project management, and CI pipeline scripts belong to DevOps. A glossary and stakeholder map are typical RE artifacts.

questions.prompt: Which TWO are IREB ELICITATION TECHNIQUES?
options: Fagan inspection.
Field observation.
Perspective-based reading.
Requirements workshop.
questions.explanation: Field observation and requirements workshops elicit requirements. Fagan inspection and perspective-based reading are review techniques.

questions.prompt: Which TWO statements correctly describe NEGOTIATION in the RE process?
options: Negotiation aims to resolve conflicting stakeholder requirements.
Negotiation is a formal review process with defined roles and minutes.
Its outcome is a solution or prioritization acceptable to the stakeholders.
Negotiation is relevant only in agile projects.
questions.explanation: Negotiation resolves stakeholder conflicts and seeks an acceptable outcome. A formal review is a different activity, and negotiation is relevant in all development approaches.

questions.prompt: Which TWO statements correctly describe PERSPECTIVE-BASED READING (PBR) as a review technique?
options: Each reviewer adopts a defined perspective, such as tester, architect, or end user.
The author moderates the review from the author’s perspective.
Different perspectives uncover different classes of defects.
All reviewers examine the document without specific role assignments.
questions.explanation: PBR assigns reviewers defined professional perspectives; each perspective focuses on different defect types. The author does not moderate their own review, and unassigned reading is not PBR.

questions.prompt: Which TWO belong in a TEXTUAL USE-CASE DESCRIPTION rather than a use-case diagram?
options: The main flow (happy path), described step by step.
Relationships between use cases (include/extend).
Preconditions that must be met before the use case starts.
Actors and the system boundary.
questions.explanation: The main flow and preconditions belong in the textual description. Use-case diagrams show actors, system boundary, and structural relationships such as include and extend.

questions.prompt: Which TWO statements correctly describe the ITERATIVE nature of the RE process according to IREB?
options: Activities such as elicitation, documentation, and validation are repeated in cycles.
The RE process is strictly sequential; each phase is performed exactly once.
Validation results may lead to further elicitation of requirements.
An iterative RE process is possible only in agile software development.
questions.explanation: The RE process is iterative: elicitation, documentation, and validation recur, and validation may trigger new elicitation. Iteration is not limited to agile projects.

questions.prompt: Domain experts can barely verbalize their knowledge. Which TWO elicitation techniques are especially suitable?
options: Structured interview with a questionnaire.
Field observation (ethnography)—observe experts at work.
Brainstorming—experts generate ideas in a group.
Prototyping—an early prototype lets experts react concretely.
questions.explanation: Field observation directly reveals what experts do, while prototyping lets them respond to a concrete model. Both avoid relying solely on verbalizing tacit knowledge.

questions.prompt: Which TWO measures directly and concretely improve requirement quality?
options: Replace vague terms with measurable thresholds (for example, ‘fast’ with ‘≤2 seconds’).
Combine all requirements into one long sentence to avoid redundancy.
Split multi-part requirements into separate atomic requirements.
Document requirements only with diagrams.
questions.explanation: Quantifying vague terms improves testability; splitting multi-part requirements improves atomicity. Combining requirements harms atomicity, and diagrams-only documentation is not an IREB rule.

questions.prompt: After an informal walkthrough, a more thorough review is needed. Which TWO statements are correct when selecting the next review type?
options: A formal Fagan inspection has the highest defect-detection rate but requires structured preparation and follow-up.
A technical review is suitable only for source code, not requirements documents.
A technical review can be used by experts to assess the technical correctness of requirements.
A formal inspection is less effort than other review forms.
questions.explanation: Formal inspection is thorough but more resource-intensive. Technical reviews can assess technical feasibility and correctness in requirements documents; they are not limited to source code.

questions.prompt: In negotiation between two stakeholder groups with conflicting requirements, which TWO principles are useful?
options: The requirements engineer unilaterally decides which requirement to adopt.
Both sides explain their underlying interests, not only their stated positions.
Document the compromise or prioritization decision transparently.
The stakeholder with the largest budget automatically takes precedence.
questions.explanation: Understanding underlying interests can reveal solutions that meet both parties’ needs. Documenting the result supports accountability and traceability and helps prevent the conflict from reappearing later.

questions.prompt: A stakeholder requests a change to an approved requirement mid-project. Which TWO change-management steps are essential?
options: Immediately edit the specification to save time.
Analyze the change’s impact on requirements, tests, and architecture.
Approve the change through a defined process, such as a Change Control Board.
Ask the stakeholder to withdraw the request in writing.
questions.explanation: Impact analysis reveals dependencies across requirements and downstream artifacts. Formal approval ensures changes are consciously decided. Editing immediately bypasses the change process.

questions.assertion: A requirement containing the word ‘and’ may fail the atomicity criterion.
questions.reason: An atomic requirement describes exactly one property or capability; ‘and’ may indicate that multiple conditions have been bundled.
questions.explanation: Both statements are correct, and the reason explains the assertion: ‘and’ often links separate properties in one requirement, violating atomicity.

questions.assertion: Validation and verification in requirements engineering are synonyms for the same review activity.
questions.reason: Both activities help ensure the quality of requirements and implementations.
questions.explanation: The assertion is false: validation checks whether requirements reflect stakeholder needs; verification checks whether implementation conforms to the specification. The reason is generally true but does not explain the false assertion.

questions.assertion: Prototyping helps externalize stakeholders’ tacit knowledge.
questions.reason: During prototyping, stakeholders spontaneously produce complete and final requirements that need no further refinement.
questions.explanation: The assertion is true: reactions to a concrete model can reveal tacit knowledge. The reason is false: prototype feedback is raw material that must be analyzed, structured, and refined. Prototyping is iterative.

questions.assertion: A sequence diagram is suitable for modeling an object’s different states and events that trigger transitions between them.
questions.reason: Sequence diagrams show the chronological order of messages between objects or components.
questions.explanation: The assertion is false: state machines model states and transitions. The reason is true—sequence diagrams show message order—but that does not make them suitable for state modeling.

questions.assertion: A requirement is complete as soon as it contains a measurable threshold.
questions.reason: Completeness requires all information necessary to implement the requirement to be present.
questions.explanation: The assertion is false: a threshold may support testability but does not guarantee completeness. The reason is true and describes the broader completeness criterion, so it does not support the assertion.

questions.assertion: Requirements workshops are suitable for resolving conflicts directly between stakeholders.
questions.reason: In a workshop, stakeholders can discuss differing requirements directly and work toward agreement.
questions.explanation: Both statements are correct, and the reason explains the assertion: workshops bring stakeholders together so they can negotiate conflicts directly.

questions.assertion: The system context contains relevant external actors, systems, and regulations.
questions.reason: In IREB, the system context and the system itself are identical because both belong to the project domain.
questions.explanation: The assertion is correct: context includes relevant external influences. The reason is false; the system boundary explicitly separates the system from its external context.

questions.assertion: Requirements workshops are effective for building shared understanding and consensus.
questions.reason: Requirements workshops can be held either in person or online.
questions.explanation: Both statements are true, but the reason does not explain the assertion. Consensus comes from direct stakeholder interaction, not from whether the meeting is in person or online.

questions.assertion: A state machine is suitable for modeling system behavior through states and transitions.
questions.reason: State machines explicitly show which events or conditions trigger a change of system state.
questions.explanation: Both statements are correct, and the reason explains the assertion: state machines represent states and the triggers for transitions between them.

questions.assertion: Prioritizing requirements helps teams implement the most important items first when resources are limited.
questions.reason: Prioritization replaces requirements validation because only the most important requirements need to be checked.
questions.explanation: The assertion is correct: prioritization helps allocate limited resources. The reason is false; prioritization never replaces validation. Any requirement that is implemented still needs validation.

questions.assertion: Quality requirements describe only a system’s performance and throughput characteristics.
questions.reason: Performance is always the most important quality attribute for every type of system.
questions.explanation: Both statements are false. Quality requirements cover many attributes, including reliability, security, usability, maintainability, availability, and portability. The most important attributes depend on the system domain.

questions.assertion: A structured interview with prepared questions is suitable for collecting comparable answers from multiple stakeholders.
questions.reason: A standardized questionnaire allows answers from different stakeholders to be compared directly.
questions.explanation: Both statements are correct, and the reason explains the benefit: asking everyone the same questions enables direct comparison of answers.

questions.assertion: Requirements traceability supports change management in a project.
questions.reason: Requirement IDs and traceability matrices are tools used to establish traceability.
questions.explanation: Both statements are true, but the reason does not explain why traceability supports change management. The key is that links reveal which artifacts may be affected by a change.

questions.assertion: The RE core activities—elicitation, documentation, review, and management—can be performed iteratively and in parallel.
questions.reason: In agile projects, requirements are documented exclusively as user stories, so other forms are not permitted.
questions.explanation: The assertion is correct: RE activities are iterative and may overlap. The reason is false; agile projects may use stories, acceptance criteria, use cases, models, and other documentation forms.

questions.assertion: An author-led review, in which the author reads their own document aloud, detects defects at the same rate as a formal inspection.
questions.reason: Formal inspections systematically detect more defects than walkthroughs and informal reviews.
questions.explanation: The assertion is false: author-led walkthroughs generally detect fewer defects because authors may overlook their own errors. The reason is correct and helps explain why the assertion is false.

questions.assertion: Requirements derived from legal or regulatory rules are often constraints that restrict the solution space.
questions.reason: Legal rules prescribe what a system must or must not do and are not freely changeable by the development team.
questions.explanation: Both statements are correct, and the reason explains the classification: legal requirements are external restrictions that the solution must satisfy.

questions.assertion: External systems can appear as actors in a use-case diagram.
questions.reason: External systems are actors because they are inside the system boundary and communicate with internal modules.
questions.explanation: The assertion is correct if the external system is outside the system boundary and interacts with the system. The reason is false: actors are outside the boundary; a system inside it is part of the system, not an actor.

questions.assertion: Acceptance criteria make user stories testable and clarify expectations between the Product Owner and development team.
questions.reason: Acceptance criteria define concrete conditions that must be met for a user story to be considered done.
questions.explanation: Both statements are correct, and the reason explains how testability is achieved: concrete done conditions allow objective checking and reduce interpretation gaps.

questions.assertion: Impact analysis is an important part of change management.
questions.reason: Traceability links between requirements and other artifacts are used when conducting impact analysis.
questions.explanation: Both statements are true, but the reason does not explain why impact analysis is important. It describes a tool used to perform it; impact analysis is important because it reveals dependencies and prevents uncontrolled change effects.

questions.assertion: A requirement is testable if it is documented in a formal template.
questions.reason: Testability means fulfillment can be determined objectively and demonstrably.
questions.explanation: The assertion is false: a template improves structure but does not make a requirement testable. The reason is correct; measurable criteria and test conditions are needed regardless of format.

questions.assertion: A traceability matrix is a typical RE artifact.
questions.reason: A traceability matrix is created in RE to link requirements to other artifacts such as design, tests, and sources.
questions.explanation: Both statements are correct, and the reason explains the classification: a traceability matrix is a work product created in RE to support management and traceability.

questions.assertion: A baseline is an agreed and reviewed requirements state against which changes are formally managed.
questions.reason: After a baseline is agreed, requirement changes are permanently prohibited and rejected.
questions.explanation: The assertion is correct: a baseline provides a reference for controlled change management. The reason is false; changes remain possible but must go through the formal change process.

questions.assertion: Consistent use of modal verbs (‘must’, ‘should’, ‘may’) in a requirements specification is important for clarity and binding force.
questions.reason: ‘Must/shall’ marks mandatory requirements, ‘should’ recommended ones, and ‘may’ optional ones; this distinction has legal and project consequences.
questions.explanation: Both statements are correct, and the reason explains why consistency matters: the modal verbs express different levels of obligation, so inconsistent use creates ambiguity.

questions.assertion: Requirements management tools support requirement versioning, status tracking, and traceability.
questions.reason: Requirements management tools automatically generate test cases from requirement text.
questions.explanation: The assertion is correct: RM tools focus on management, versioning, status, and traceability. The reason is false; automatic test-case generation is not a standard RM-tool function.

questions.assertion: A stakeholder map (for example, an onion diagram) helps identify all relevant stakeholders.
questions.reason: An onion diagram places stakeholders in concentric rings according to their proximity to the system.
questions.explanation: Both statements are true, but the concentric-ring layout does not explain why stakeholder maps help identify stakeholders. Their systematic visualization draws attention to groups that might otherwise be missed.

questions.assertion: Perspective-based reading increases defect detection in requirements reviews.
questions.reason: Different perspectives, such as tester, designer, and operator, reveal defect types that may be missed from a single perspective.
questions.explanation: Both statements are correct, and the reason explains the mechanism: each role looks for relevant issues, and combining perspectives provides broader coverage than undirected reading.

questions.assertion: Untestable requirements make it substantially harder to derive test cases.
questions.reason: Untestable requirements are always shorter than testable ones and therefore cannot be used as a basis for test cases.
questions.explanation: The assertion is correct: without objective conditions, meaningful test cases cannot be derived. The reason is false; requirement length has no direct relationship to testability.

questions.assertion: A requirement describes a condition or capability that a system must have to meet a contract, standard, or specification.
questions.reason: Requirements can come from different stakeholders with different interests and priorities.
questions.explanation: Both statements are true, but the diversity of stakeholder interests does not explain the definition of a requirement; it is a separate observation.

questions.assertion: In a formal inspection, the author must not also act as moderator.
questions.reason: Separating the author and moderator helps prevent the author’s own perspective from biasing the review and overlooking defects.
questions.explanation: Both statements are correct, and the reason explains the role separation: an independent moderator supports objective discussion and recording of findings.

questions.assertion: According to IREB Syllabus v3.0, design is one of the four core RE activities.
questions.reason: Good system design is based on clearly documented requirements.
questions.explanation: The assertion is false: IREB’s four core activities are elicitation, documentation, validation/review, and management. Design belongs to systems engineering. The reason is true but does not make design an RE core activity.

questions.assertion: An <<include>> relationship in a use-case diagram represents mandatory inclusion.
questions.reason: <<include>> is used when two use cases share an actor and therefore must be merged.
questions.explanation: The assertion is correct: <<include>> is mandatory. The reason is false; shared actors are unrelated. The base use case includes another when it needs that use case to achieve its goal.

questions.assertion: In agile projects, requirements are elicited and refined iteratively rather than fully specified in advance.
questions.reason: The Agile Manifesto values working software over comprehensive documentation.
questions.explanation: Both statements are correct, but the manifesto’s preference for working software does not explain iterative elicitation. Iteration is also driven by requirements being incomplete or uncertain at the start and becoming clearer through feedback and learning.

questions.assertion: The GDPR is a typical element of the system context for software that processes personal data.
questions.reason: The GDPR is outside the system boundary and imposes external requirements the development team must satisfy but cannot change.
questions.explanation: Both statements are correct, and the reason explains why GDPR belongs to the context: it is external to the system and imposes requirements that the system must meet.

questions.assertion: Unambiguity means a requirement permits exactly one interpretation.
questions.reason: Using formal mathematical notation automatically guarantees unambiguity.
questions.explanation: The assertion is correct. The reason is false: formal notation can reduce ambiguity but does not automatically eliminate it; symbols or predicates may still be undefined or unclear.

questions.assertion: Bidirectional traceability (forward and backward) is more valuable than unidirectional traceability.
questions.reason: Bidirectional traceability requires more effort to maintain links.
questions.explanation: Both statements are true, but maintenance effort does not explain the greater value. Bidirectional links support both impact analysis forward and source justification backward.

questions.assertion: Requirements negotiation should be facilitated by a neutral moderator.
questions.reason: A neutral moderator helps prevent one stakeholder from dominating and ensures all perspectives are heard.
questions.explanation: Both statements are correct, and the reason explains the value of neutral moderation: it helps address power imbalances and gives less influential stakeholders a safe opportunity to contribute.

questions.assertion: Stakeholder requirements describe needs at a more abstract level than system requirements.
questions.reason: Stakeholder requirements are always incomplete and must therefore be replaced by system requirements.
questions.explanation: The assertion is correct: stakeholder requirements express needs at a higher level; system requirements make them more concrete. The reason is false: stakeholder requirements are not inherently incomplete; they are at a different abstraction level and are refined, not replaced.

questions.assertion: A user story is complete as soon as it follows the format ‘As [role], I want [goal], so that [benefit].’
questions.reason: The user-story format guarantees that the story is testable and implementable.
questions.explanation: Both statements are false. The format alone does not ensure completeness; acceptance criteria, clarity, and appropriate size are also needed. The format does not guarantee testability or implementability.

questions.assertion: Prototyping can be used to validate requirements.
questions.reason: Prototypes can be created cheaply as low-fidelity paper prototypes.
questions.explanation: Both statements are true, but low cost does not explain why prototypes support validation. Stakeholders can interact with a model and judge whether it matches their expectations.

questions.assertion: Every requirement should have a unique identification number (ID).
questions.reason: Without unique IDs, requirements cannot be referenced precisely in traceability matrices, test plans, and change requests.
questions.explanation: Both statements are correct, and the reason explains the purpose of IDs: precise reference. Without unique IDs, searching and linking requirements becomes error-prone.

questions.assertion: A stakeholder map should include indirect stakeholders such as regulators and system operators.
questions.reason: Indirect stakeholders often have binding requirements that may be discovered late and cause costly specification changes.
questions.explanation: Both statements are correct, and the reason explains the assertion: identifying indirect stakeholders early helps discover regulatory, operational, and interface requirements before they cause costly rework.

questions.assertion: A context diagram shows the system being developed as a black box and its external interfaces with the environment.
questions.reason: Context diagrams describe the system’s internal structure to help developers orient themselves quickly.
questions.explanation: The assertion is correct: a context diagram shows the system as one undifferentiated unit and its external entities and flows. The reason is false; internal details are intentionally excluded and shown in more detailed models.

questions.assertion: In a formal inspection, the author may act as moderator to answer content questions directly.
questions.reason: The author knows the document best and can immediately clarify reviewer misunderstandings.
questions.explanation: The assertion is false: the author and moderator must be separate roles to avoid bias and undue influence. The reason may be true, but the author’s familiarity does not justify moderating their own document.

questions.assertion: Formal inspections collect defect metrics to optimize the review process and make document quality measurable.
questions.reason: Measuring defect density and severity allows quality trends to be tracked across inspections and improvements targeted.
questions.explanation: Both statements are correct, and the reason explains how metrics support optimization: trends across inspections reveal recurring weaknesses and opportunities for improvement.

questions.assertion: A baseline and requirements versioning are the same concept in IREB.
questions.reason: Both are used to document the historical state of requirements.
questions.explanation: The assertion is false: versioning continuously tracks changes, while a baseline is a formally agreed snapshot used as a reference for change management. The reason is broadly true but does not make the concepts identical.

questions.assertion: A requirement’s ‘source’ attribute identifies the stakeholder or document from which it originated.
questions.reason: Knowing the source makes it possible to contact the right person when questions or conflicts arise.
questions.explanation: Both statements are correct, and the reason explains the practical value of source information: it supports follow-up communication when requirements change or conflict.

questions.assertion: An entity-relationship diagram (ERD) models a system’s static data structures, including entities, attributes, and relationships.
questions.reason: An ERD shows how data is structured at a point in time, not how it changes over time.
questions.explanation: Both statements are correct, and the reason explains the ERD’s static nature: it describes data structure without a time or process dimension, complementing behavioral models.

questions.assertion: Stakeholder requirements describe what stakeholders need from a system, while system requirements describe what the system must do to meet those needs.
questions.reason: System requirements are derived from stakeholder requirements and are usually more detailed and precise.
questions.explanation: Both statements are correct, and the reason explains the abstraction hierarchy: system requirements refine stakeholder needs into more concrete, measurable statements.

questions.assertion: Validation in requirements engineering checks whether requirements correctly reflect stakeholders’ actual needs.
questions.reason: Without validation, a system can be built correctly according to its specification and still fail to solve the users’ real problem.
questions.explanation: Both statements are correct, and the reason explains the practical consequence: if the specification does not reflect real needs, even a correct implementation may deliver the wrong system.

questions.assertion: Regulatory authorities can be stakeholders even if they never use the system directly.
questions.reason: Stakeholders include people, groups, or organizations interested in requirements or affected by the system’s impacts.
questions.explanation: Both statements are correct, and the reason explains the assertion: stakeholder status depends on interest, influence, or impact, not direct system use.

questions.assertion: Requirements that combine several conditions with ‘and’ should be split into separate atomic requirements.
questions.reason: Atomic requirements can be tested, prioritized, and managed independently.
questions.explanation: Both statements are correct, and the reason explains the practical benefit of atomicity: separate requirements can be independently tested, prioritized, and changed.

questions.assertion: A baseline prevents requirements from being changed after approval.
questions.reason: Baselines provide an agreed reference point from which changes can be traced through a controlled process.
questions.explanation: The assertion is false: a baseline does not prohibit changes; it controls them. The reason correctly describes a baseline’s purpose.

questions.assertion: The ‘W’ in MoSCoW means a requirement is permanently excluded from the project.
questions.reason: MoSCoW is a scope-management tool that categorizes requirements by urgency for the current release.
questions.explanation: The assertion is false: ‘Won’t have this time’ means deferred from the current release, not permanently excluded. The reason correctly describes MoSCoW’s release focus.

questions.assertion: Functional requirements describe WHAT a system should do—its services, functions, and behavior.
questions.reason: Quality (non-functional) requirements describe HOW WELL the system performs its functions.
questions.explanation: Both statements are correct, but the reason describes a complementary category rather than explaining why functional requirements describe behavior. Functional requirements arise from stakeholder goals and tasks.

questions.assertion: Negotiation is needed when two stakeholders have conflicting requirements for the same system.
questions.reason: Negotiation aims for a solution accepted by all involved stakeholders, rather than imposing one stakeholder’s requirements on another.
questions.explanation: Both statements are correct, and the reason explains why negotiation is needed: the goal is an accepted consensus or compromise, not one party’s victory.

questions.assertion: A use-case diagram shows the detailed flow of every scenario in a use case.
questions.reason: The textual use-case description contains the main flow, alternative flows, preconditions, and postconditions.
questions.explanation: The assertion is false: a use-case diagram provides only a structural overview of actors, use cases, and relationships. The reason is true; flow details belong in the textual description.

questions.assertion: An unverifiable requirement such as ‘The system should be user-friendly’ must be revised before it can serve as a basis for development and testing.
questions.reason: Verifiability requires an objective test for each requirement, for example through measurable thresholds or acceptance criteria.
questions.explanation: Both statements are correct, and the reason explains why: a requirement must have objective criteria so its fulfillment can be tested. Vague requirements cannot be reliably implemented or verified.

questions.assertion: The system boundary separates the system being developed from its context, so context elements are not under the development team’s direct control.
questions.reason: Everything outside the system boundary belongs to the system context and must be treated as a given condition.
questions.explanation: Both statements are correct, and the reason explains the assertion: the boundary distinguishes controllable system elements from external context that must be treated as given.

questions.assertion: Requirements can be prioritized using methods such as MoSCoW, the Kano model, or value analysis.
questions.reason: Prioritization should be performed exclusively by the requirements engineer without stakeholder involvement.
questions.explanation: The assertion is correct: several prioritization methods exist. The reason is false because stakeholders must contribute business value and urgency judgments; the RE can facilitate but should not decide alone.

questions.assertion: Functional requirements and constraints both describe externally visible system behavior from the user’s perspective.
questions.reason: Both requirement types influence what the system can ultimately provide to users.
questions.explanation: The assertion is false: functional requirements describe system behavior, while constraints restrict the solution space. The reason is generally true but does not support the false assertion.

questions.assertion: Contradictions between requirements should be resolved before the specification is baselined.
questions.reason: Unresolved contradictions can force developers to make arbitrary decisions and lead to inconsistent system behavior.
questions.explanation: Both statements are correct, and the reason explains why contradictions should be resolved before baselining: otherwise implementation decisions may be made ad hoc, creating quality problems.

questions.assertion: Requirements workshops are useful for developing a shared understanding of the problem.
questions.reason: Requirements workshops can last from two hours to several days.
questions.explanation: Both statements are true, but workshop duration does not explain why workshops foster shared understanding. The reason is direct, simultaneous exchange among stakeholders.

questions.assertion: Use cases can be documented both graphically (use-case diagram) and textually (scenario description).
questions.reason: A use-case diagram shows every detailed interaction step between actor and system.
questions.explanation: The assertion is correct: use cases have graphical and textual representations. The reason is false; diagrams provide an overview, while detailed interaction steps belong in the textual scenario.

questions.assertion: In requirements engineering, verification checks whether documented requirements match actual stakeholder needs.
questions.reason: Verification ensures that the system was developed according to the agreed specification.
questions.explanation: The assertion is false: checking requirements against stakeholder needs is validation. The reason is correct for verification, which checks implementation against specification.

questions.assertion: Field observation is particularly suitable for uncovering stakeholders’ tacit knowledge.
questions.reason: Field observation lets the RE observe stakeholders in their real work environment, revealing actual workflows and unspoken practices.
questions.explanation: Both statements are correct, and the reason explains the mechanism: observing real work reveals routines, workarounds, and implicit rules that stakeholders may not be able to verbalize.

questions.assertion: A requirements specification should be validated before implementation begins.
questions.reason: Techniques such as prototyping, reviews, and formal methods are available for validating requirements.
questions.explanation: Both statements are correct, but the availability of techniques does not explain why validation should precede implementation. The reason is risk reduction: requirement defects are cheaper to correct before implementation.

questions.assertion: A walkthrough is less formal than an inspection.
questions.reason: In a walkthrough, an external independent moderator leads the meeting to ensure maximum objectivity.
questions.explanation: The assertion is correct: walkthroughs are less formal and do not require structured preparation or defect metrics. The reason is false; the author presents the document, and an external moderator is not required.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly describes VALIDATION in requirements engineering?
options: Validation checks whether implementation conforms to the specification.
Validation checks whether the specification meets actual stakeholder needs—‘Are we building the RIGHT system?’
Validation checks a requirements document’s internal consistency for contradictions.
Validation is performed only through automated tests after implementation.
questions.explanation: Validation asks whether the specification reflects stakeholders’ real needs. Verification asks whether the implementation conforms to the specification. This is a key distinction in RE.

questions.prompt: Which question represents VERIFICATION?
options: Are we building the RIGHT system?
Are we building the system RIGHT?
Are we reviewing the right stakeholders?
Are we documenting requirements completely?
questions.explanation: Verification asks, ‘Are we building the system RIGHT?’—implementation versus specification. Validation asks, ‘Are we building the RIGHT system?’—specification versus stakeholder needs.

questions.prompt: ‘Building the RIGHT system’ refers to:
options: Verification.
Validation.
Inspection.
Technical review.
questions.explanation: Validation asks whether the system addresses actual stakeholder needs. Verification asks whether the implementation conforms to the specification.

questions.prompt: When should requirements ideally be VALIDATED?
options: Only at the end of the project after full implementation.
Early and continuously, beginning with initial requirement drafts.
Only when an external formal review is required.
Only after all verification activities are complete.
questions.explanation: Validate as early as possible. Defects found in requirements early are much cheaper to correct than after implementation. Prototypes, reviews, and workshops support early validation.

questions.prompt: Which review technique does NOT require structured individual preparation by reviewers?
options: Formal inspection (Fagan inspection).
Walkthrough.
Checklist-based technical review.
Peer review with defect log.
questions.explanation: A walkthrough does not require formal preparation: the author presents the document and reviewers give spontaneous feedback. A Fagan inspection requires an individual preparation phase.

questions.prompt: Which review technique achieves the HIGHEST defect-detection rate?
options: Informal review.
Walkthrough.
Technical review.
Formal inspection (Fagan inspection).
questions.explanation: Formal inspection typically has the highest defect-detection rate because it requires individual preparation, defined roles, checklists, structured meetings, and defect metrics. Informal techniques are quicker but less thorough.

questions.prompt: Which technique is an IREB-recognized VALIDATION technique?
options: Syntax checking with a parser.
Formal inspection with defect metrics.
Prototyping with stakeholder feedback.
Automated regression testing.
questions.explanation: Prototyping supports validation because stakeholders interact with an early model and assess whether it meets their needs. Formal inspection checks artifact quality; syntax checks and regression tests are technical verification activities.

questions.prompt: ‘Reviews check whether the system works correctly.’ This statement is:
options: Correct—reviews are the most important form of system quality assurance.
Incorrect—reviews inspect written artifacts such as requirements or design without executing the system.
Correct—reviews and dynamic tests are equivalent.
Incorrect—reviews are used only in agile projects.
questions.explanation: Reviews are static techniques: people inspect artifacts without executing the system. Tests are dynamic and run the system. Equating reviews with tests is a common misconception.

questions.prompt: Which TOOL CATEGORY is primarily used to create UML and BPMN diagrams?
options: Requirements management tool such as DOORS or Polarion.
Modeling tool such as Enterprise Architect or Visual Paradigm.
Test management tool such as TestRail or Zephyr.
Configuration management tool such as Git.
questions.explanation: Modeling tools support graphical notations such as UML, BPMN, and ERD. Requirements-management tools focus on requirement versioning, traceability, and status, with more limited modeling support.

questions.prompt: What can REQUIREMENTS MANAGEMENT TOOLS (RM tools) NOT automatically ensure?
options: Requirement versioning and change history.
Traceability links between requirements and test cases.
The content quality and correctness of requirements.
Status tracking for each requirement.
questions.explanation: RM tools manage, link, and version requirements, but poor requirements remain poor requirements. Content quality depends on RE competence, process, and human reviews; the tool does not replace the RE process.
